records.prompt: 60% is equivalent to ___.
records.gist: Convert 60 percent to a fraction, then reduce to lowest terms. Percent means per hundred.
keywords: identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: identify the equipment, location, and requirement. Start with General knowledge, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three formulas run the math questions. Ohm's law: volts = amps × ohms. Power: watts = volts × amps (so amps = watts ÷ volts). Resistors in parallel combine as the product over the sum. Voltage drop percent is volts lost ÷ source volts. And AC frequency: 60 cycles per second means one full 360° wave takes 1/60 s. To turn a percent into a fraction, write it over 100 and reduce.

This is a straight math conversion — no NEC lookup needed. Numbers in the question: 60%. Convert the given value and match it to the equal choice.

LOOKUP FOCUS
identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.reference_text:
Basic Trade Math — Percent to Fraction Conversion
60% = 60 / 100 = 6 / 10 = 3 / 5.
records.tip_short: Percent means per hundred: write 60 over 100, then reduce to 3/5. Correct: B — 3/5. 60 over 100 reduces by dividing both by 20, giving 3/5. Not A: 5/8 is 62.5 percent, slightly more than 60 percent. Not C: 2/5 is 40 percent, the remainder after 60 percent. Not D: 5/16 is about 31 percent, far less than 60 percent.
records.formula: Percent / 100 = Fraction
records.worked: 60% = 60/100. Divide numerator and denominator by 20 to get 3/5.
choice_notes: 5/8 is 62.5 percent, slightly more than 60 percent.
60 over 100 reduces by dividing both by 20, giving 3/5.
2/5 is 40 percent, the remainder after 60 percent.
5/16 is about 31 percent, far less than 60 percent.

408.18(C) Connections
Each section of equipment that requires rear or side access to make field connections shall be so marked by the manufacturer on the front. Section openings requiring rear or side access shall comply with 110.26. Load terminals for field wiring shall comply with 408.18(C)(1), (C)(2), or (C)(3) as applicable.

records.prompt: Refer to the figure below. GIVEN: Switch S1 is in the "ON" position, but the light does not come on. Voltage across L1 is measured to be 120 volts. Voltage across S1 is measured to be 0 volts. The light does not come on because ___.
answers: the light is open (bulb burned out)
the light and switch are shorted
the light is good but the switch does not make contact
there is a break in the wiring of the circuit
records.gist: There are 0 volts across the switch and full voltage across the lamp, yet the lamp is dark; each reading narrows the fault location.
keywords: identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: identify the equipment, location, and requirement. Start with General knowledge, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
A switch is rated for what it interrupts. Ordinary snap switches handle lighting loads, but inductive loads like motors and ballasts punish contacts, so the NEC caps them at half the switch's ampere rating. A three-way switch is secretly a single-pole double-throw — one lever flipping power between two traveler paths, which is why two of them team up to control one light from two places.

This asks which switch rule fits. Numbers in the question: 120 volts, 0 volts. Check whether the question is about the ampere rating, the type of load, or where and how the switch is installed.

LOOKUP FOCUS
identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.reference_text:
Switch and Lamp Troubleshooting
With S1 closed and 0 volts measured across it, the switch contacts are conducting. With the full 120 volts appearing across the lamp terminals, the open is inside the lamp itself (a burned-out filament), so no current flows in the circuit.
records.tip_short: Full voltage appears across the open part: 120 volts across the lamp with the switch closed means the lamp is open. Correct: A — the light is open (bulb burned out). With 0 volts across the closed switch and 120 volts across the lamp, the lamp filament is open. Not B: A short would read near 0 volts across the shorted part and likely trip the breaker, not show 120 volts. Not C: A switch that failed to make contact would show 120 volts across the switch, not 0 volts. Not D: A wiring break would put the voltage across the break, so the lamp would read 0 volts.
choice_notes: With 0 volts across the closed switch and 120 volts across the lamp, the lamp filament is open.
A short would read near 0 volts across the shorted part and likely trip the breaker, not show 120 volts.
A switch that failed to make contact would show 120 volts across the switch, not 0 volts.
A wiring break would put the voltage across the break, so the lamp would read 0 volts.

records.prompt: Where multiple driven ground rods are used to form the grounding electrode system, in order to maintain an effective grounding electrode system, they shall not be less than ___ apart.

records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS

Three jobs, three parts. Grounding connects the system to the earth (rods, plates, concrete-encased electrodes) to drain lightning and surges. Bonding joins all the metal parts together so fault current has a fast low-resistance road back to the source that trips the breaker. The grounded conductor (neutral, white) carries normal current; the grounding conductor (green/bare) carries only fault current. The main bonding jumper is where neutral and ground meet — at the service, and only there.

WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
A GFCI watches the current going out and coming back on a circuit. If even a tiny amount leaks — say, through a person to ground — it trips in a fraction of a second. That is why the NEC demands GFCI protection anywhere water and electricity can meet: bathrooms, kitchens, garages, outdoors, crawl spaces, laundry areas, pools, and spas.

records.prompt: For an arc welder with an I1max rating of 43 amps, what is the maximum rating for the overcurrent device supplying the welder?

records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Overcurrent protection works in layers. The branch breaker or fuse handles violent short circuits and ground faults and must carry the motor's starting surge without tripping. Delicate internals — luminaire ballasts, appliance circuits, control wiring — get smaller supplementary protectors, but those never replace branch-circuit protection. Where staying online matters, selective coordination stages the devices so only the faulted circuit goes dark.

LOOKUP FOCUS

records.reference_text:
630.12 Overcurrent Protection
Overcurrent protection for arc welders shall be as provided in 630.12(A) and (B). Where the values as determined by this section do not correspond to the standard ampere ratings provided in 240.6 or where the rating or setting specified results in unnecessary opening of the overcurrent device, the next higher standard rating or setting shall be permitted.
(A) For Welders
Each welder shall have overcurrent protection rated or set at not more than 200 percent of I1max. Alternatively, if the I1max is not given, the overcurrent protection shall be rated or set at not more than 200 percent of the rated primary current of the welder.
An overcurrent device shall not be required for a welder that has supply conductors protected by an overcurrent device rated or set at not more than 200 percent of I1max or at the rated primary current of the welder.

Correct: B — 90 amp. 200 percent of 43 amperes is 86 amperes; 630.12 permits the next higher standard size, 90 amperes. Not A: 85 amperes is below the 86 amperes computed (200 percent of 43) and is not a standard 240.6 size. Not C: 95 amperes is not a standard 240.6 rating and exceeds the next size up from 86 amperes. Not D: 100 amperes skips past 90 amperes, the next standard size above the 86 amperes calculated.
records.formula: Welder overcurrent device ≤ 200% of I1max (630.12(A)). If that is not a standard rating, 630.12 permits the next higher standard rating (240.6(A) ratings rise by 10 A from 60 A to 110 A).

records.prompt: Fuel dispensing systems shall be provided with one or more clearly identified emergency shutoff devices or electrical disconnects. Such disconnects or devices shall be installed in approved locations but not less than 20 feet or more than ___ feet from the fuel dispensing devices that they serve.
records.gist: Fuel dispensing areas require an emergency shutoff that is reachable during a fire yet positioned away from the hazard. Twenty feet is given as the near limit. The question asks the far limit.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: disconnecting means. Start with 514.11(A), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
A disconnecting means is simply the switch or breaker a worker opens before touching equipment. The golden rule is 'within sight': visible and no more than 50 ft away, so nobody can re-energize it unseen. Motors need a disconnect in sight of both the controller and the motor itself; appliances and AC units need one in sight and quickly reachable. If the disconnect must live far away, it has to be lockable open with the location marked on the equipment.

This is a maximum-limit question. Numbers in the question: 20 feet. The correct choice is the maximum value the NEC allows — eliminate any choice on the wrong side of that limit.

records.reference_text:
514.11(A) Emergency Electrical Disconnects
Fuel dispensing systems shall be provided with one or more clearly identified emergency shutoff devices or electrical disconnects. Such devices or disconnects shall be installed in approved locations but not less than 6 m (20 ft) or more than 30 m (100 ft) from the fuel dispensing devices that they serve. Emergency shutoff devices or electrical disconnects shall disconnect power to all dispensing devices; to all remote pumps serving the dispensing devices; to all associated power, control, and signal circuits; and to all other electrical equipment in the hazardous (classified) locations surrounding the fuel dispensing devices. When more than one emergency shutoff device or electrical disconnect is provided, all devices shall be interconnected. Resetting from an emergency shutoff condition shall require manual intervention and the manner of resetting shall be approved by the authority having jurisdiction. [30A:6.7] The emergency shutoff device shall disconnect simultaneously from the source of supply, all conductors of the circuits, including the grounded conductor, if any. Equipment grounding conductors shall remain connected.

Not C: 80 feet is not the limit; the maximum distance in 514.11(A) is 100 feet.

WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS

A motor circuit has two separate protections doing two jobs. The overload device (heaters, overload relay) guards against a motor slowly cooking from too much load — sized from the motor's own nameplate amps (125% for sturdy motors, 115% for the rest), with one overload unit per phase (three units on a three-phase motor). The breaker or fuses handle violent short circuits and ground faults. The controller starts and stops the motor; the disconnect within sight of the motor lets a worker be sure it cannot restart while hands are on it.

Provided with a marked "off" position
Directly open all ungrounded conductors when manually placed in the "off" position

records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three formulas run the math questions. Ohm's law: volts = amps × ohms. Power: watts = volts × amps (so amps = watts ÷ volts). Resistors in parallel combine as the product over the sum. Voltage drop percent is volts lost ÷ source volts. And AC frequency: 60 cycles per second means one full 360° wave takes 1/60 s. To turn a percent into a fraction, write it over 100 and reduce.

This is a straight math conversion — no NEC lookup needed. Convert the given value and match it to the equal choice.

records.reference_text:
Switch Terminology & Classification • Three-Way Switches
A standard three-way switch connects a common terminal to either of two traveler terminals. In standard electrical switch configuration terminology, this single-pole, double-throw mechanism is designated as an SPDT switch.
records.tip_short: A three-way switch has one common terminal flipping between two travelers: single pole, double throw. Correct: D — SPDT. A three-way connects one common terminal to either of two travelers, which is single pole, double throw. Not A: DPST switches two conductors on and off together and has no traveler positions. Not B: DPDT switches two poles between two paths, closer to a four-way switch than a three-way. Not C: SPST is a simple on-off single-pole switch with no second throw position.

DPDT switches two poles between two paths, closer to a four-way switch than a three-way.

records.prompt: Which of the following is a flexible cord type that is permitted in a wet location and is sunlight resistant?
records.gist: Flexible cord type letters tell where a cord may be used. The question asks which one of these four types is a flexible cord rated for wet locations that is also sunlight resistant.
keywords: identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: identify the equipment, location, and requirement. Start with Table 400.4, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Flexible cords are temporary wiring, not a substitute for fixed circuits — they must stay continuous (no splices except repairing hard-service cord), stay short, and match the job's toughness: junior hard-service (SJ) for light duty, hard-service (S, ST) for tools and appliances. The letters on a cord are a code: S = hard service, J = junior hard service (300 V), T = thermoplastic, O = oil-resistant jacket, OO = oil-resistant jacket and insulation, W = wet locations and sunlight resistant. Building wires such as THWN and XHWN also carry a W (wet location), but they are single conductors for raceways, not flexible cords, and Table 400.4 does not list them.

In plain terms, the question is: "Which of the following is a flexible cord type that is permitted in a wet location and is sunlight resistant?"

Read the situation, then test each choice against it. Eliminate choices that contradict the stated conditions; the survivor that fits all of them is the answer.

LOOKUP FOCUS
identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.reference_text:
Table 400.4 Flexible Cords and Flexible Cables, Note 9
Cords that comply with the requirements for outdoor cords and are so listed shall be permitted to be designated as weather and water resistant with the suffix "W" after the Code type designation. Cords with the "W" suffix are suitable for use in wet locations and are sunlight resistant.

records.prompt: One or more metal in-ground support structure(s) in direct contact with the earth vertically for ___ feet or more, with or without concrete encasement is a permitted grounding electrode.
records.gist: A structural steel column in contact with earth may serve as an electrode only with sufficient earth contact. The question asks how many feet must be in the earth.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: grounding electrode. Start with NEC 250.52(A)(2), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three jobs, three parts. Grounding connects the system to the earth (rods, plates, concrete-encased electrodes) to drain lightning and surges. Bonding joins all the metal parts together so fault current has a fast low-resistance road back to the source that trips the breaker. The grounded conductor (neutral, white) carries normal current; the grounding conductor (green/bare) carries only fault current. The main bonding jumper is where neutral and ground meet — at the service, and only there.

This asks you to name the grounding or bonding part in this installation. Subject: grounding electrode. Trace the fault-current path: what connects the equipment back to the source?

LOOKUP FOCUS
grounding electrode
records.reference_text:
250.52(A)(2) Metal In-Ground Support Structure(s)
One or more metal in-ground support structure(s) in direct contact with the earth vertically for 3.0 m (10 ft) or more, with or without concrete encasement. If multiple metal in-ground support structures are present at a building or a structure, it shall be permissible to bond only one into the grounding electrode system.
Informational Note: Metal in-ground support structures include, but are not limited to, pilings, casings, and other structural metal.
records.tip_short: Metal pilings or structural steel in earth vertically for 10 feet or more count as a grounding electrode. Correct: C — 10. 250.52(A)(2) requires direct contact with the earth vertically for 3.0 m (10 feet) or more. Not A: 6 feet is too short; 250.52(A)(2) requires 3.0 m (10 feet) or more. Not B: 8 feet is the minimum ground rod length, not the in-ground support structure length. Not D: 12 feet exceeds the minimum; the Code requires 10 feet or more.
choice_notes: 6 feet is too short; 250.52(A)(2) requires 3.0 m (10 feet) or more.
8 feet is the minimum ground rod length, not the in-ground support structure length.
250.52(A)(2) requires direct contact with the earth vertically for 3.0 m (10 feet) or more.
12 feet exceeds the minimum; the Code requires 10 feet or more.

WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS

Services and transformers are about size and labels. A one-family dwelling service from 100–400 A may use conductors smaller than the service rating (the diversity of a home makes full size unnecessary). Every transformer must wear a nameplate with its ratings — but not trivia like the wire gauge inside it. And transformers generally need a disconnect in sight, or lockable with its location marked on the unit.

answers: for wiring in wet, dry, or corrosive locations
records.gist: Type UF cable is rated for wet, dry, and corrosive soil conditions. The question asks where the Code lets you run it, and three of these answers are places it forbids.

records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: cable. Start with 340.10(3), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Decode the letters first: MI = Mineral-Insulated (wires in white mineral powder inside a copper tube — fireproof, for hazardous and harsh spots). MC = Metal-Clad (metal armor, goes almost anywhere). NM = Nonmetallic-sheathed, Romex (dry homes only). UF = Underground Feeder (burial and wet spots). SE = Service-Entrance (brings power in). AC = Armored Cable/BX (grounds through its armor plus a bonding strip, needs a red anti-short bushing). USE stays buried outside and may not come indoors.

records.reference_text:
340.10 Uses Permitted
Type UF cable shall be permitted as follows:
(1) For use underground, including direct burial in the earth.
(2) As single-conductor cables. Where installed as single-conductor cables, all conductors of the feeder or branch circuit, including the grounded conductor and equipment grounding conductor, if any, shall be installed in accordance with 300.3.
(3) For wiring in wet, dry, or corrosive locations.
(4) Installed as nonmetallic-sheathed cable. Where so installed, the installation and conductor requirements shall comply with Parts II and III of Article 334, except for 334.12(B), and shall be of the multiconductor type.
(5) As single-conductor cables as the nonheating leads for heating cables as provided in 424.43.
(6) Supported by cable trays. Type UF cable supported by cable trays shall be of the multiconductor type.
Informational Note: See 310.14(A)(3) for temperature limitation of conductors.

Not B: Type UF is not permitted in commercial garages. Not C: 340.12 does not permit Type UF where subject to physical damage.

records.prompt: A controller that includes motor overload protection ___ for group motor application shall be marked with the motor overload protection and the maximum branch-circuit short-circuit and ground-fault protection for such applications.
records.gist: A controller serving a motor group must display a marking identifying its protection. The question asks which word the Code requires in that marking.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: ground fault, motor, load calculation. Start with 430.8, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Overcurrent protection works in layers. The branch breaker or fuse handles violent short circuits and ground faults and must carry the motor's starting surge without tripping. Delicate internals — luminaire ballasts, appliance circuits, control wiring — get smaller supplementary protectors, but those never replace branch-circuit protection. Where staying online matters, selective coordination stages the devices so only the faulted circuit goes dark.

This is a maximum-limit question. Subject: motor. The correct choice is the maximum value the NEC allows — eliminate any choice on the wrong side of that limit.

A motor controller that includes motor overload protection suitable for group motor application shall be marked with the motor overload protection and the maximum branch-circuit short-circuit and ground-fault protection for such applications.
Combination motor controllers that employ adjustable instantaneous trip circuit breakers shall be clearly marked to indicate the ampere settings of the adjustable trip element.
records.tip_short: Controllers with overload protection suitable for group motors must be marked with overload and max protection ratings. Correct: D — suitable. 430.8 refers to motor overload protection suitable for group motor application. Not A: Required is not the Code word; 430.8 describes overload protection suitable for group motor application. Not B: Recognized is not the Code word; 430.8 uses suitable. Not C: Permitted is not the Code word; 430.8 uses suitable.

records.prompt: The permitted demand factor for five household clothes dryers in a multifamily dwelling is ___.
records.gist: Multiple household dryers do not operate simultaneously, so a demand factor applies. The question asks what share five of them count as.
records.article_title: Branch-Circuit, Feeder, and Service Load Calculations
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: dwelling unit. Start with Table 220.54, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Load calculations never just add everything up, because a home never runs all loads at once. Start with 3 VA per square foot of living space (outside dimensions, minus open porches and unfinished spaces), add 1,500 VA for each small-appliance and laundry circuit, then shrink the subtotal with the demand factor (first 3,000 VA at full value, 3,001 to 120,000 VA at 35%, the remainder at 25%). Ranges and dryers use their own tables — a range nameplate is only the starting point. Heat and AC: count the larger one, never both.

In plain terms, the question is: "The permitted demand factor for five household clothes dryers in a multifamily dwelling is ___." Subject: dwelling unit. Break it into pieces — what equipment, what location or measurement, and what the NEC must say about it — then find the choice that satisfies every piece.

LOOKUP FOCUS
dwelling unit
records.reference_text:
Table 220.54 Demand Factors for Household Electric Clothes Dryers
Number of Dryers	Demand Factor (%)
1-4	100%
5	85%
6	75%
7	65%
8	60%
9	55%
10	50%
11	47%
12-23	47% minus 1% for each dryer exceeding 11
24-42	35% minus 0.5% for each dryer exceeding 23
43 and over	25%

Table 220.54 assigns an 85 percent demand factor to five household dryers. Not A: 70 percent is not a Table 220.54 value for any dryer count from 5 to 11; 6 dryers are 75 percent and 7 are 65 percent. Not B: 75 percent is the Table 220.54 demand factor for 6 dryers, not 5. Not C: 80 percent is not a Table 220.54 value; the factor drops from 85 percent at 5 dryers to 75 percent at 6.
records.formula: Multiple dryers use the Table 220.54 demand factor for that dryer count.

records.prompt: A stop switch is wired ___ in a motor circuit.
records.gist: A motor stop device must directly open the control circuit, which requires a specific wiring configuration. The question asks which way.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: motor. Start with General knowledge, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
A motor circuit has two separate protections doing two jobs. The overload device (heaters, overload relay) guards against a motor slowly cooking from too much load — sized from the motor's own nameplate amps (125% for sturdy motors, 115% for the rest), with one overload unit per phase (three units on a three-phase motor). The breaker or fuses handle violent short circuits and ground faults. The controller starts and stops the motor; the disconnect within sight of the motor lets a worker be sure it cannot restart while hands are on it.

This asks you to match this motor or transformer setup to its rule. Subject: motor. Identify whether the question is about protection size, conductor size, disconnect location, or marking.

LOOKUP FOCUS
motor
records.reference_text:
Motor Control Circuits • Control Station Wiring
A stop pushbutton switch has normally closed (NC) contacts that must open the control circuit to de-energize the magnetic holding coil. Therefore, the stop switch is always wired in series with the motor control circuit.
records.tip_short: Stop buttons are normally closed and wired in series, so pressing any one breaks the holding coil circuit. Correct: A — series. The normally closed stop button is in series, so opening it drops out the holding coil. Not B: Series-shunt describes motor field windings, not how a stop button is connected. Not C: Series-parallel is wrong; multiple stop buttons all go in series, while start buttons go in parallel. Not D: Parallel is how start buttons connect; a stop button in parallel could not break the control circuit.
choice_notes: The normally closed stop button is in series, so opening it drops out the holding coil.
Series-shunt describes motor field windings, not how a stop button is connected.
Series-parallel is wrong; multiple stop buttons all go in series, while start buttons go in parallel.
Parallel is how start buttons connect; a stop button in parallel could not break the control circuit.

records.prompt: Where no GFCI protection is provided, the mounting height of a paddle fan located above a spa or hot tub shall not be less than ___ feet.

records.article_title: Swimming Pools, Fountains, and Similar Installations
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: ground-fault circuit-interrupter. Start with 680.43(B)(1)(a), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
A GFCI watches the current going out and coming back on a circuit. If even a tiny amount leaks — say, through a person to ground — it trips in a fraction of a second. That is why the NEC demands GFCI protection anywhere water and electricity can meet: bathrooms, kitchens, garages, outdoors, crawl spaces, laundry areas, pools, and spas.

This is a minimum-limit question. Subject: hot tub. The correct choice is the minimum value the NEC allows — eliminate any choice on the wrong side of that limit.

(a) Without GFCI. Where no GFCI protection is provided, the mounting height shall be not less than 3.7 m (12 ft).
(b) With GFCI. Where GFCI protection is provided, the mounting height shall be permitted to be not less than 2.3 m (7 ft 6 in.).
(c) Below 2.3 m (7 ft 6 in.). Luminaires meeting the requirements of item (1) or (2) and protected by a ground-fault circuit interrupter shall be permitted to be installed less than 2.3 m (7 ft 6 in.) over a spa or hot tub:
(1) Recessed luminaires with a glass or plastic lens, nonmetallic or electrically isolated metal trim, and suitable for use in damp locations
(2) Surface-mounted luminaires with a glass or plastic globe, a nonmetallic body, or a metallic body isolated from contact, and suitable for use in damp locations

WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS

Flexible cords are temporary wiring, not a substitute for fixed circuits — they must stay continuous (no splices except repairing hard-service cord), stay short, and match the job's toughness: junior hard-service (SJ) for light duty, hard-service (S, ST) for tools and appliances, extra-hard (SO) for construction sites. The letters are a code: O = oil-resistant, T = thermoplastic, W = weather/wet-location plus sunlight-resistant. A cord in a wet place outdoors needs that W — which is why STOOW is the answer there.

The length of the cord is not less than 450 mm (18 in.) and not exceeding 900 mm (36 in.).
Receptacles are located to protect against physical damage to the flexible cord.
The receptacle is accessible.
The flexible cord has an equipment grounding conductor and is terminated with a grounding-type attachment plug.

records.gist: Convert 40 percent to a fraction and reduce to lowest terms.
keywords: identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: identify the equipment, location, and requirement. Start with General knowledge, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three formulas run the math questions. Ohm's law: volts = amps × ohms. Power: watts = volts × amps (so amps = watts ÷ volts). Resistors in parallel combine as the product over the sum. Voltage drop percent is volts lost ÷ source volts. And AC frequency: 60 cycles per second means one full 360° wave takes 1/60 s. To turn a percent into a fraction, write it over 100 and reduce.

This is a straight math conversion — no NEC lookup needed. Numbers in the question: 40%. Convert the given value and match it to the equal choice.

LOOKUP FOCUS
identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.reference_text:
Basic Trade Math — Percent to Fraction Conversion
40% = 40 / 100 = 4 / 10 = 2 / 5.
records.tip_short: Percent to fraction: write it over 100 and reduce, so 40/100 becomes 2/5. Correct: C — 2/5. 40 percent is 40/100, which reduces to 2/5. Not A: 5/8 equals 62.5 percent, not 40 percent. Not B: 3/5 equals 60 percent, not 40 percent. Not D: 5/16 equals 31.25 percent, not 40 percent.
records.formula: Percent / 100 = Fraction
records.worked: 40% = 40/100. Divide numerator and denominator by 20 to get 2/5.
choice_notes: 5/8 equals 62.5 percent, not 40 percent.
3/5 equals 60 percent, not 40 percent.
40 percent is 40/100, which reduces to 2/5.
5/16 equals 31.25 percent, not 40 percent.

406.12 Tamper-Resistant Receptacles
All 15- and 20-ampere, 125- and 250-volt nonlocking-type receptacles in the following locations shall be listed tamper-resistant receptacles:
All dwelling units, boathouses, mobile homes and manufactured homes, including their attached and detached garages, accessory buildings, and common areas
Guest rooms and guest suites of hotels, motels, and their common areas
Child care facilities
Preschools and education facilities
Within clinics, medical and dental offices, and outpatient facilities, the following spaces:
Business offices accessible to the general public
Lobbies, and waiting spaces
Spaces of nursing homes and limited care facilities covered in 517.10(B)(2)
Places of awaiting transportation, gymnasiums, skating rinks, fitness centers, and auditoriums
Dormitory units
Residential care/assisted living facilities, social and substance abuse rehabilitation facilities, and group homes

records.reference_text:
800.44(B) Above Roofs
Communications wires and cables and CATV-type coaxial cables shall have a vertical clearance of not less than 2.5 m (8 ft) from all points of roofs above which they pass.
Exception No. 1: Communications wires and cables and CATV-type coaxial cables shall not be required to have a vertical clearance of not less than 2.5 m (8 ft) above auxiliary buildings, such as garages and the like.
Exception No. 2: A reduction in clearance above only the overhanging portion of the roof to not less than 450 mm (18 in.) shall be permitted if (1) not more than 1.2 m (4 ft) of communications and CATV-type service-drop conductors pass above the roof overhang and (2) they are terminated at a through- or above-the-roof raceway or approved support.

records.prompt: Where equipment rated 800 amperes or more that contains overcurrent devices is installed and there is a personnel door intended for entrance to and egress from the working space less than ___ feet from the nearest edge of the working space, the door shall open at least 90 degrees in the direction of egress and be equipped with listed panic hardware or listed fire exit hardware.

records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: overcurrent protection. Start with 110.26(C)(3), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Working space is the empty bubble an electrician stands in while servicing live gear — nobody may store boxes or park equipment in it. The NEC measures it three ways: depth in front (3+ ft depending on voltage and what faces the gear — concrete or brick walls facing you mean deeper space), 30 in. minimum width (or the equipment's width), and 6-1/2 ft of headroom. Big gear needs doors that swing 90° and a way out that open doors can't block. Above panels, the space up to the ceiling belongs to electrics only — no pipes or ducts.

records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
A disconnecting means is simply the switch or breaker a worker opens before touching equipment. The golden rule is 'within sight': visible and no more than 50 ft away, so nobody can re-energize it unseen. Motors need a disconnect in sight of both the controller and the motor itself; appliances and AC units need one in sight and quickly reachable. If the disconnect must live far away, it has to be lockable open with the location marked on the equipment.

records.prompt: Flexible cords shall be used only in continuous lengths, without splices, other than splices for the repair of hard-service cord or ___ cord under certain conditions.
records.gist: Flexible cord splices are generally prohibited, with repair permitted only for specified hard-service cord types. The question asks which other cord type the Code also names for repair.
keywords: identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: identify the equipment, location, and requirement. Start with NEC 400.13, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Flexible cords are temporary wiring, not a substitute for fixed circuits — they must stay continuous (no splices except repairing hard-service cord), stay short, and match the job's toughness: junior hard-service (SJ) for light duty, hard-service (S, ST) for tools and appliances, extra-hard (SO) for construction sites. The letters are a code: O = oil-resistant, T = thermoplastic, W = weather/wet-location plus sunlight-resistant. A cord in a wet place outdoors needs that W — which is why STOOW is the answer there.

In plain terms, the question is: "Flexible cords shall be used only in continuous lengths, without splices, other than splices for the repair of hard-service cord or ___…" Break it into pieces — what equipment, what location or measurement, and what the NEC must say about it — then find the choice that satisfies every piece.

Flexible cord shall be used only in continuous lengths without splice or tap where initially installed in applications permitted by 400.10(A). 300.4(D) Cables and Raceways Parallel to Framing Members and Furring Strips
In both exposed and concealed locations, where a cable- or raceway-type wiring method is installed parallel to framing members, such as joists, rafters, or studs, or is installed parallel to furring strips, the cable or raceway shall be installed and supported so that the nearest outside surface of the cable or raceway is not less than 32 mm (1 1/4 in.) from the nearest edge of the framing member or furring strips where nails or screws are likely to penetrate. records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS

records.prompt: You have 125 volts at the panel and 115 volts at the load. What is the percentage of voltage drop?

records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three formulas run the math questions. Ohm's law: volts = amps × ohms. Power: watts = volts × amps (so amps = watts ÷ volts). Resistors in parallel combine as the product over the sum. Voltage drop percent is volts lost ÷ source volts. And AC frequency: 60 cycles per second means one full 360° wave takes 1/60 s. To turn a percent into a fraction, write it over 100 and reduce.

VD = V_source - V_load = 125V - 115V = 10V drop.
% Voltage Drop = (10V / 125V) * 100 = 8%.

records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three formulas run the math questions. Ohm's law: volts = amps × ohms. Power: watts = volts × amps (so amps = watts ÷ volts). Resistors in parallel combine as the product over the sum. Voltage drop percent is volts lost ÷ source volts. And AC frequency: 60 cycles per second means one full 360° wave takes 1/60 s. To turn a percent into a fraction, write it over 100 and reduce.

records.reference_text:
Electrical Theory • Ohmmeter Readings
An open resistor has a break in its resistive path, so the small test current from the ohmmeter's battery cannot flow through it. The meter therefore shows infinite resistance (OL on a digital meter, or a needle that does not move). A reading of zero ohms indicates a short; a reading within tolerance indicates a good resistor.

Electrical Theory • Transformer Turns Ratio
A transformer ratio of 20:1 is read primary to secondary: 20 primary turns for every 1 secondary turn. Voltage divides in the same proportion (Es ÷ Ep = Ns ÷ Np), so the secondary voltage is 1/20 of the primary voltage, while current changes in the inverse ratio.

Electrical Theory • Series Circuits and Lamp Resistance
A lamp's resistance is R = E² ÷ P, so a 25-watt lamp has more resistance than a 60-watt lamp (at 120 volts about 576 ohms versus 240 ohms). In a series circuit the same current flows through every part and is set by the total resistance. Swapping in the higher-resistance 25-watt lamp raises the total resistance and lowers the current, so the heater's output (I² × R) decreases.
records.tip_short: A lower-wattage lamp has higher resistance; in series it cuts the current for everything, so the heater puts out less heat. Correct: A — heater output will decrease. The 25-watt lamp has higher resistance, so the series current drops and the heater's output (I squared times R) decreases. Not B: Output would rise only if total resistance dropped; the 25-watt lamp adds resistance and reduces the current. Not C: Current still flows around the series loop, so the lamp still glows, just dimly. Not D: Changing a series element changes the current, so the heater output cannot stay the same.

Electrical Theory • Phase Angle (ELI the ICE Man)
In an inductive circuit the voltage (E) leads the current (I): ELI. In a capacitive circuit the current (I) leads the voltage (E): ICE. A lagging current therefore means the circuit is inductive. At resonance the inductive and capacitive reactances cancel and the current is in phase with the voltage.

Electrical Theory • Effective (RMS) Value
The effective, or root-mean-square (RMS), value of a sine wave is the value that produces the same heating as the same amount of direct current. It equals 0.707 times the peak value. Meters, nameplates, and the NEC use effective values: 120 volts ac means 120 volts RMS.

Resistance is proportional to length and inversely proportional to cross-sectional area (R = K × L ÷ A). Tripling the length multiplies the resistance by 3, and halving the area multiplies it by 2.
records.tip_short: Resistance rises with length and falls with area: triple the length and halve the area and the resistance goes up six times. Correct: C — 30Ω. Not A: 7.5 ohms matches no correct step; tripling the length and halving the area multiplies 5 ohms by 6. Not B: 15 ohms accounts only for the tripled length; halving the area doubles the resistance again. Not D: 50 ohms overshoots; the combined factor is 3 times 2, or 6, so 5 ohms becomes 30 ohms.
records.formula: R = K × L ÷ A: resistance rises in proportion to length and in inverse proportion to cross-sectional area. Apply both changes to the original 5 ohms.

Three jobs, three parts. Grounding connects the system to the earth (rods, plates, concrete-encased electrodes) to drain lightning and surges. Bonding joins all the metal parts together so fault current has a fast low-resistance road back to the source that trips the breaker. The grounded conductor (neutral, white) carries normal current; the grounding conductor (green/bare) carries only fault current. The main bonding jumper is where neutral and ground meet — at the service, and only there.

records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: conduit. Start with 358.30(A), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Decode the letters first: EMT = Electrical Metallic Tubing (thin-wall, hand-bendable). RMC = Rigid Metal Conduit (thick threaded steel). IMC = Intermediate (in between). FMC = Flexible Metal Conduit (bendable whip). ENT = Electrical Nonmetallic Tubing (blue smurf tube). LFMC = Liquidtight Flexible Metal (sealed whip). RNC = Rigid Nonmetallic Conduit (PVC). Rules answer three things: clearance from wood framing (1-1/4 in. or a nail plate), burial depth, and strapping (within a foot of every box, then every few feet by type).

This asks which wiring-method rule fits this installation. Subject: conduit. Numbers in the question: 3 feet. Focus on whether the question is about support spacing, fill, burial cover, protection from damage, or where the method is permitted.

LOOKUP FOCUS
conduit
records.reference_text:
358.30(A) Securely Fastened
EMT shall be securely fastened in place in accordance with the following:
At intervals not to exceed 3 m (10 ft)
Within 900 mm (3 ft) of each outlet box, junction box, device box, cabinet, conduit body, or other tubing termination
Exception No. 1: Fastening of unbroken lengths shall be permitted to be increased to a distance of 1.5 m (5 ft) where structural members do not readily permit fastening within 900 mm (3 ft).
Exception No. 2: For concealed work in finished buildings or prefinished wall panels where such securing is impracticable, unbroken lengths (without coupling) of EMT shall be permitted to be fished.
records.tip_short: EMT support: within 3 feet of boxes and every 10 feet, stretched to 5 feet where framing prevents 3 feet. Correct: B — 5'. 358.30(A) Exception No. 1 allows unbroken lengths to be fastened within 1.5 m (5 feet). Not A: 4 feet is not in 358.30(A); the exception extends the 3 foot limit to 5 feet. Not C: 6 feet exceeds the 5 foot maximum permitted by 358.30(A) Exception No. 1. Not D: 10 feet is the maximum spacing between EMT supports, not the distance from a termination.
choice_notes: 4 feet is not in 358.30(A); the exception extends the 3 foot limit to 5 feet.
358.30(A) Exception No. 1 allows unbroken lengths to be fastened within 1.5 m (5 feet).
6 feet exceeds the 5 foot maximum permitted by 358.30(A) Exception No. 1.
10 feet is the maximum spacing between EMT supports, not the distance from a termination.

records.prompt: What is the maximum cord-and-plug connected load permitted on a 15 amp receptacle that is supplied by a 20 amp circuit supplying multiple outlets?
records.gist: A receptacle on a circuit rated higher than itself has a cap on the cord-and-plug load it may carry. The question asks that cap for a 15-amp receptacle on a 20-amp multi-outlet circuit.
records.article_title: Branch Circuits Not Over 1000 Volts AC, 1500 Volts DC, Nominal
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: receptacle outlet, load calculation. Start with Table 210.21(B)(2), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Flexible cords are temporary wiring, not a substitute for fixed circuits — they must stay continuous (no splices except repairing hard-service cord), stay short, and match the job's toughness: junior hard-service (SJ) for light duty, hard-service (S, ST) for tools and appliances, extra-hard (SO) for construction sites. The letters are a code: O = oil-resistant, T = thermoplastic, W = weather/wet-location plus sunlight-resistant. A cord in a wet place outdoors needs that W — which is why STOOW is the answer there.

This is a maximum-limit question. Subject: receptacle. Numbers in the question: 15 amp, 20 amp. The correct choice is the maximum value the NEC allows — eliminate any choice on the wrong side of that limit.

LOOKUP FOCUS
receptacle outlet, load calculation
records.reference_text:
Table 210.21(B)(2) Maximum Cord-and-Plug-Connected Load to Receptacle
Circuit Rating (Amperes) | Receptacle Rating (Amperes) | Maximum Load (Amperes)
15 or 20 | 15 | 12
20 | 20 | 16
30 | 30 | 24
records.tip_short: Cord load on a receptacle is 80 percent of its rating: a 15 ampere receptacle gets 12 amperes. Correct: A — 12 amps. Table 210.21(B)(2) limits a 15 ampere receptacle on a 20 ampere circuit to 12 amperes. Not B: 16 amperes is the limit for a 20 ampere receptacle on a 20 ampere circuit, not a 15 ampere one. Not C: 20 amperes is the circuit rating; cord load on the 15 ampere receptacle is limited to 12 amperes. Not D: 24 amperes exceeds both the receptacle and circuit ratings; the table limit is 12 amperes.
choice_notes: Table 210.21(B)(2) limits a 15 ampere receptacle on a 20 ampere circuit to 12 amperes.
16 amperes is the limit for a 20 ampere receptacle on a 20 ampere circuit, not a 15 ampere one.
20 amperes is the circuit rating; cord load on the 15 ampere receptacle is limited to 12 amperes.
24 amperes exceeds both the receptacle and circuit ratings; the table limit is 12 amperes.

records.prompt: Enclosures for overcurrent protection devices must be mounted in a/an ___ position.
records.gist: Overcurrent device enclosures have a required mounting orientation, with only limited exceptions. The question asks which orientation is required.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: overcurrent protection, cable. Start with 240.33, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Overcurrent protection works in layers. The branch breaker or fuse handles violent short circuits and ground faults and must carry the motor's starting surge without tripping. Delicate internals — luminaire ballasts, appliance circuits, control wiring — get smaller supplementary protectors, but those never replace branch-circuit protection. Where staying online matters, selective coordination stages the devices so only the faulted circuit goes dark.

In plain terms, the question is: "Enclosures for overcurrent protection devices must be mounted in a/an ___ position." Break it into pieces — what equipment, what location or measurement, and what the NEC must say about it — then find the choice that satisfies every piece.

LOOKUP FOCUS
overcurrent protection, cable
records.reference_text:
240.33 Vertical Position
Enclosures for overcurrent devices shall be mounted in a vertical position. Circuit breaker enclosures shall be permitted to be installed horizontally where the circuit breaker is installed in accordance with 240.81. Listed busway plug-in units shall be permitted to be mounted in orientations corresponding to the busway mounting position.
records.tip_short: Overcurrent device enclosures mount vertically; horizontal breaker mounting is allowed only per 240.81. Correct: B — vertical. 240.33 states enclosures for overcurrent devices shall be mounted in a vertical position. Not A: 240.33 requires vertical mounting; horizontal is allowed only for breakers installed per 240.81. Not C: Perspective is a drawing term, not a mounting position recognized in 240.33. Not D: Upright suggests vertical, but 240.33 uses the term vertical position, the intended answer.
choice_notes: 240.33 requires vertical mounting; horizontal is allowed only for breakers installed per 240.81.
240.33 states enclosures for overcurrent devices shall be mounted in a vertical position.
Perspective is a drawing term, not a mounting position recognized in 240.33.
Upright suggests vertical, but 240.33 uses the term vertical position, the intended answer.

records.prompt: Heat generated internally in the conductor as the result of load current flow, including fundamental and ___ currents.
records.gist: Conductor temperature depends partly on heat generated by the load current itself, and the rule names two components of that current. The question asks the one besides the fundamental.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: load calculation. Start with 310.14(A)(3)(2), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Load calculations never just add everything up, because a home never runs all loads at once. Start with 3 VA per square foot of living space (outside dimensions, minus open porches and unfinished spaces), add 1,500 VA for each small-appliance and laundry circuit, then shrink the subtotal with the demand factor (first 3,000 VA at full value, 3,001 to 120,000 VA at 35%, the remainder at 25%). Ranges and dryers use their own tables — a range nameplate is only the starting point. Heat and AC: count the larger one, never both.

In plain terms, the question is: "Heat generated internally in the conductor as the result of load current flow, including fundamental and ___ currents." Break it into pieces — what equipment, what location or measurement, and what the NEC must say about it — then find the choice that satisfies every piece.

LOOKUP FOCUS
load calculation
records.reference_text:
310.14(A)(3) Temperature Limitation of Conductors
No conductor shall be used in such a manner that its operating temperature exceeds that designated for the type of insulated conductor involved. In no case shall conductors be associated together in such a way, with respect to type of circuit, the wiring method employed, or the number of conductors, that the limiting temperature of any conductor is exceeded.
Informational Note No. 1: See Table 310.4(1) and Table 315.10(A) for the temperature rating of a conductor that is the maximum temperature, at any location along its length, that the conductor can withstand over a prolonged time period without serious degradation. The ampacity tables of Article 310 and the ampacity tables of Informative Annex B, the ambient temperature correction factors in 310.15(B), and the notes to the tables provide guidance for coordinating conductor sizes, types, ampacities, ambient temperatures, and number of associated conductors. The principal determinants of operating temperature are as follows:
(1) Ambient temperature - ambient temperature may vary along the conductor length as well as from time to time.
(2) Heat generated internally in the conductor as the result of load current flow, including fundamental and harmonic currents.
(3) The rate at which generated heat dissipates into the ambient medium. Thermal insulation that covers or surrounds conductors affects the rate of heat dissipation.
(4) Adjacent load-carrying conductors - adjacent conductors have the dual effect of raising the ambient temperature and impeding heat dissipation.
Informational Note No. 2: Refer to 110.14(C) for the temperature limitation of terminations.
records.tip_short: Conductor heating comes from load current, including fundamental and harmonic currents. Correct: C — harmonic. 310.14(A)(3) says internal heat comes from load current, including fundamental and harmonic currents. Not A: Dissipation is how heat leaves the conductor, listed separately in 310.14(A)(3). Not B: Alternation is not a current type named in 310.14(A)(3). Not D: Transfer is not a current type named in 310.14(A)(3).
choice_notes: Dissipation is how heat leaves the conductor, listed separately in 310.14(A)(3).
Alternation is not a current type named in 310.14(A)(3).
310.14(A)(3) says internal heat comes from load current, including fundamental and harmonic currents.
Transfer is not a current type named in 310.14(A)(3).

records.prompt: Equipment grounding conductors must be the same size as the circuit conductors for ___ amp circuits.
records.gist: For small circuits, the minimum equipment grounding conductor from the sizing table matches the usual circuit wire size. The question asks which of these circuit ratings that is true for.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: equipment grounding conductor, conductors. Start with Table 250.122, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three jobs, three parts. Grounding connects the system to the earth (rods, plates, concrete-encased electrodes) to drain lightning and surges. Bonding joins all the metal parts together so fault current has a fast low-resistance road back to the source that trips the breaker. The grounded conductor (neutral, white) carries normal current; the grounding conductor (green/bare) carries only fault current. The main bonding jumper is where neutral and ground meet — at the service, and only there.

This asks you to name the grounding or bonding part in this installation. Trace the fault-current path: what connects the equipment back to the source?

LOOKUP FOCUS
equipment grounding conductor, conductors
records.reference_text:
Table 250.122 Minimum Size Equipment Grounding Conductors for Grounding Raceway and Equipment
Rating or Setting of Automatic Overcurrent Device in Circuit Ahead of Equipment, Conduit, etc., Not Exceeding (Amperes)	Size (AWG or kcmil) Copper	Aluminum or Copper-Clad Aluminum
15	14	12
20	12	10
60	10	8
100	8	6
reference_table: NOTE: Size from the rating or setting of the overcurrent device ahead of the circuit, not from the circuit conductor size. A rating between rows uses the next larger row.
records.tip_short: At 15, 20, and 30 amperes, the Table 250.122 copper EGC (14, 12, 10 AWG) matches the usual circuit wire size. Correct: D — all of these. At 15, 20, and 30 amperes the Table 250.122 copper EGC equals the circuit conductor size. Not A: True for 30 amperes (10 AWG EGC with 10 AWG wire), but 15 and 20 ampere circuits match too. Not B: True for 20 amperes (12 AWG EGC with 12 AWG wire), but 15 and 30 ampere circuits match too. Not C: True for 15 amperes (14 AWG EGC with 14 AWG wire), but 20 and 30 ampere circuits match too.
choice_notes: True for 30 amperes (10 AWG EGC with 10 AWG wire), but 15 and 20 ampere circuits match too.
True for 20 amperes (12 AWG EGC with 12 AWG wire), but 15 and 30 ampere circuits match too.
True for 15 amperes (14 AWG EGC with 14 AWG wire), but 20 and 30 ampere circuits match too.
At 15, 20, and 30 amperes the Table 250.122 copper EGC equals the circuit conductor size.

records.prompt: When supplying a room air conditioner rated 120 volts, the length of the flexible supply cord must not exceed ___.
records.gist: Room air conditioners may be cord-connected, and the maximum cord length depends on the voltage rating. The question asks the limit at 120 volts.
keywords: identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: identify the equipment, location, and requirement. Start with 440.64, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Appliances play by cord-and-plug rules: a kitchen disposer may use a short flexible cord (18 in. to 3 ft) instead of hard wiring, and a room air conditioner gets a short cord matched to its voltage (about 10 ft at 120 V, 6 ft at 240 V). Big fixed appliances — ranges, dryers, water heaters — skip simple nameplate math and use their own demand tables, and laundry always gets its own dedicated 20-amp circuit.

In plain terms, the question is: "When supplying a room air conditioner rated 120 volts, the length of the flexible supply cord must not exceed ___." Numbers in the question: 120 volts. Break it into pieces — what equipment, what location or measurement, and what the NEC must say about it — then find the choice that satisfies every piece.

LOOKUP FOCUS
identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.reference_text:
440.64 Supply Cords
Where a flexible cord is used to supply a room air conditioner, the length of such cord shall not exceed 3.0 m (10 ft) for a nominal, 120-volt rating or 1.8 m (6 ft) for a nominal, 208- or 240-volt rating.
records.tip_short: Room air conditioner cords: up to 10 feet at 120 volts, but only 6 feet at 208 or 240 volts. Correct: C — 10 feet. 440.64 limits the cord to 3.0 m (10 feet) for a nominal 120 volt room air conditioner. Not A: 6 feet is the 440.64 limit for 208 or 240 volt units, not 120 volt units. Not B: 8 feet is not a 440.64 limit; 120 volt units may have up to 10 feet of cord. Not D: 12 feet exceeds the 10 foot maximum in 440.64 for 120 volt units.
choice_notes: 6 feet is the 440.64 limit for 208 or 240 volt units, not 120 volt units.
8 feet is not a 440.64 limit; 120 volt units may have up to 10 feet of cord.
440.64 limits the cord to 3.0 m (10 feet) for a nominal 120 volt room air conditioner.
12 feet exceeds the 10 foot maximum in 440.64 for 120 volt units.

records.prompt: A ___ must be located in sight from the motor location and the driven machinery location.
records.gist: Anyone working on a motor or its driven machinery must be able to see the device that kills its power. The question asks which device must be in sight of both.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: motor, disconnecting means. Start with 430.102(B)(1), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
A motor circuit has two separate protections doing two jobs. The overload device (heaters, overload relay) guards against a motor slowly cooking from too much load — sized from the motor's own nameplate amps (125% for sturdy motors, 115% for the rest), with one overload unit per phase (three units on a three-phase motor). The breaker or fuses handle violent short circuits and ground faults. The controller starts and stops the motor; the disconnect within sight of the motor lets a worker be sure it cannot restart while hands are on it.

This asks you to match this motor or transformer setup to its rule. Subject: motor. Identify whether the question is about protection size, conductor size, disconnect location, or marking.

LOOKUP FOCUS
motor, disconnecting means
records.reference_text:
430.102(B)(1) Separate Motor Disconnect
A disconnecting means for the motor shall be located in sight from the motor location and the driven machinery location.
records.tip_short: In sight means visible and within 50 feet; the motor disconnect must be in sight of both motor and machine. Correct: A — disconnecting means. 430.102(B)(1) requires the motor disconnecting means in sight from the motor and driven machinery. Not B: A circuit breaker can serve as a disconnect, but 430.102(B)(1) names the disconnecting means. Not C: A fuse provides overcurrent protection and is not itself a disconnecting means. Not D: The controller starts and stops the motor; 430.102(B)(1) places the disconnecting means in sight.
choice_notes: 430.102(B)(1) requires the motor disconnecting means in sight from the motor and driven machinery.
A circuit breaker can serve as a disconnect, but 430.102(B)(1) names the disconnecting means.
A fuse provides overcurrent protection and is not itself a disconnecting means.
The controller starts and stops the motor; 430.102(B)(1) places the disconnecting means in sight.

records.prompt: Outdoor antennas and lead-in conductors for radio and TV equipment must not cross over open conductors of electric light or power circuits, and must be kept well away from all such circuits to avoid the possibility of accidental contact. Where proximity to open electric light or power service conductors of less than 250 volts between conductors cannot be avoided, the installation must provide a clearance of at least ___.
records.gist: Antenna lead-ins must stay clear of open power conductors to prevent accidental contact. The question asks the minimum clearance when the power conductors are under 250 volts and closeness cannot be avoided.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: conductors. Start with 810.13, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Antennas must fail without touching power lines: masts are corrosion-proof metal strong enough for ice and wind, guyed where needed, and stood well clear of any overhead conductors above 150 volts to ground. Lead-in wires get their own clearances, and the whole installation needs lightning protection — a rooftop mast is often the tallest thing around.

This is a minimum-limit question. Subject: antenna. Numbers in the question: 250 volts. The correct choice is the minimum value the NEC allows — eliminate any choice on the wrong side of that limit.

LOOKUP FOCUS
conductors
records.reference_text:
810.13 Avoidance of Contacts With Conductors of Other Systems
Outdoor antennas and lead-in conductors from an antenna to a building shall not cross over open conductors of electric light or power circuits and shall be kept well away from all such circuits so as to avoid the possibility of accidental contact. Where proximity to open electric light or power service conductors of less than 250 volts between conductors cannot be avoided, the installation shall be such as to provide a clearance of at least 600 mm (2 ft).
Where practicable, antenna conductors shall be installed so as not to cross under open electric light or power conductors.
records.tip_short: Antenna lead-ins near open power conductors under 250 volts need at least 2 feet of clearance. Correct: C — 24". 810.13 requires at least 600 mm (2 feet), which is 24 inches. Not A: 12 inches is only half the 600 mm (2 feet) clearance required by 810.13. Not B: 18 inches is less than the 2 foot clearance required by 810.13. Not D: 30 inches is more than the minimum; 810.13 requires at least 24 inches (2 feet).
choice_notes: 12 inches is only half the 600 mm (2 feet) clearance required by 810.13.
18 inches is less than the 2 foot clearance required by 810.13.
810.13 requires at least 600 mm (2 feet), which is 24 inches.
30 inches is more than the minimum; 810.13 requires at least 24 inches (2 feet).

records.prompt: Effective safe work practices are based on which of the following?
records.gist: Electrical safe work practices start from an assessment of the hazard a worker faces. The question asks what that assessment, and so the practices, are based on.
keywords: identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: identify the equipment, location, and requirement. Start with NFPA 70E, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
You cannot see electricity, so safety is a procedure, not a sense. Plan every job: identify all energy sources, lock and tag them open, verify zero voltage with a meter, and use insulated tools on anything that might be live. Treat pools, heaters, old panels, and anything unfamiliar as energized until your meter proves otherwise.

Read the situation, then test each choice against it. Eliminate choices that contradict the stated conditions; the survivor that fits all of them is the answer.

LOOKUP FOCUS
identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.reference_text:
NFPA 70E Standard for Electrical Safety in the Workplace • Safe Work Practices
Effective electrical safe work practices are based on identifying the type of hazard (shock, arc flash, arc blast), the manner of exposure (contact, proximity), and the degree of exposure (voltage, incident energy).
records.tip_short: Safe work practice asks three things: what hazard, how you are exposed, and how much exposure. Correct: D — All of these. Effective safe work practices weigh hazard type, manner of exposure, and degree of exposure together. Not A: Type of hazard, such as shock or arc flash, matters, but manner and degree of exposure count too. Not B: Manner of exposure, contact or proximity, matters, but hazard type and degree count too. Not C: Degree of exposure, voltage or incident energy, matters, but hazard type and manner count too.
choice_notes: Type of hazard, such as shock or arc flash, matters, but manner and degree of exposure count too.
Manner of exposure, contact or proximity, matters, but hazard type and degree count too.
Degree of exposure, voltage or incident energy, matters, but hazard type and manner count too.
Effective safe work practices weigh hazard type, manner of exposure, and degree of exposure together.

records.prompt: Conductors in a non-jacketed multiconductor cable, such as ribbon cable in a permanent amusement attraction shall not be smaller than ___ AWG.
records.gist: Amusement attractions use small control wiring, and unjacketed ribbon cable gets a stricter minimum size than jacketed cable. The question asks that minimum AWG size.
records.article_title: Control Systems for Permanent Amusement Attractions
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: cable, conductors. Start with 522.21(B), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Decode the letters first: MI = Mineral-Insulated (wires in white mineral powder inside a copper tube — fireproof, for hazardous and harsh spots). MC = Metal-Clad (metal armor, goes almost anywhere). NM = Nonmetallic-sheathed, Romex (dry homes only). UF = Underground Feeder (burial and wet spots). SE = Service-Entrance (brings power in). AC = Armored Cable/BX (grounds through its armor plus a bonding strip, needs a red anti-short bushing). USE stays buried outside and may not come indoors.

This asks which wiring-method rule fits this installation. Focus on whether the question is about support spacing, fill, burial cover, protection from damage, or where the method is permitted.

LOOKUP FOCUS
cable, conductors
records.reference_text:
522.21(B) Conductors Within an Enclosure or Operator Station
Conductors of size 30 AWG or larger shall be permitted in a listed and jacketed multiconductor cable within an enclosure or operator station. Conductors in a non-jacketed multiconductor cable, such as ribbon cable, shall not be smaller than 26 AWG. Single conductors shall not be smaller than 24 AWG.
Exception: Single conductors 30 AWG or larger shall be permitted for jumpers and special wiring applications.
records.tip_short: Amusement attraction wiring: jacketed cable 30 AWG, ribbon cable 26 AWG, single conductors 24 AWG. Correct: C — 26. 522.21(B) says non-jacketed multiconductor cable, such as ribbon cable, shall not be smaller than 26 AWG. Not A: 22 AWG is larger than required; 522.21(B) allows ribbon cable conductors down to 26 AWG. Not B: 24 AWG is the minimum for single conductors in 522.21(B), not for ribbon cable. Not D: 30 AWG is allowed only in listed jacketed cable or for jumpers, not in non-jacketed ribbon cable.

24 AWG is the minimum for single conductors in 522.21(B), not for ribbon cable.
522.21(B) says non-jacketed multiconductor cable, such as ribbon cable, shall not be smaller than 26 AWG.
30 AWG is allowed only in listed jacketed cable or for jumpers, not in non-jacketed ribbon cable.

records.prompt: For installations consisting of not more than two 2-wire branch circuits, the building disconnecting means must have a rating of not less than ___ amps.
records.gist: A building fed by only a couple of 2-wire branch circuits still needs a disconnect of some minimum rating. The question asks that minimum rating in amps.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: branch circuit, disconnecting means. Start with 225.39(B), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Branch circuits are rated by their breaker: the standard sizes are 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, and 50 amps. A multiwire (shared-neutral) circuit must open all its ungrounded legs together so no leg can stay live alone. And the number of circuits in a building comes from the total load divided by circuit size — fractional results always round up, because half a circuit doesn't exist.

This is a maximum-limit question. Subject: disconnecting means. The correct choice is the maximum value the NEC allows — eliminate any choice on the wrong side of that limit.

LOOKUP FOCUS
branch circuit, disconnecting means
records.reference_text:
225.39(B) Two-Circuit Installations
For installations consisting of not more than two 2-wire branch circuits, the feeder or branch-circuit disconnecting means shall have a rating of not less than 30 amperes.
records.tip_short: Building disconnect minimums: one branch circuit 15 amperes, two 2-wire branch circuits 30 amperes. Correct: D — 30. 225.39(B) requires a rating of not less than 30 amperes for two 2-wire branch circuits. Not A: 15 amperes is the 225.39(A) minimum for a single branch circuit, not two circuits. Not B: 20 amperes is not a 225.39 minimum; two 2-wire circuits require at least 30 amperes. Not C: 25 amperes is not a 225.39 value; two-circuit installations require at least 30 amperes.
choice_notes: 15 amperes is the 225.39(A) minimum for a single branch circuit, not two circuits.
20 amperes is not a 225.39 minimum; two 2-wire circuits require at least 30 amperes.
25 amperes is not a 225.39 value; two-circuit installations require at least 30 amperes.
225.39(B) requires a rating of not less than 30 amperes for two 2-wire branch circuits.

records.prompt: Supplementary overcurrent protection ___.
answers: must not be used in luminaires
may be used to protect internal circuits of equipment
may be used as a substitute for a branch-circuit overcurrent protection device
records.gist: Supplementary overcurrent devices add protection inside equipment but are not the required branch-circuit protection. The question asks which statement about them is true.

records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Overcurrent protection works in layers. The branch breaker or fuse handles violent short circuits and ground faults and must carry the motor's starting surge without tripping. Delicate internals — luminaire ballasts, appliance circuits, control wiring — get smaller supplementary protectors, but those never replace branch-circuit protection. Where staying online matters, selective coordination stages the devices so only the faulted circuit goes dark.

240.10 Supplementary Overcurrent Protection
Where supplementary overcurrent protection is used for luminaires, appliances, and other equipment or for internal circuits and components of equipment, it shall not be used as a substitute for required branch-circuit overcurrent devices or in place of the required branch-circuit protection. Supplementary overcurrent devices shall not be required to be readily accessible.

Not A: 240.10 says supplementary overcurrent devices are not required to be readily accessible. Not B: 240.10 specifically allows supplementary protection for luminaires, so it is not prohibited there. Not D: 240.10 forbids using supplementary protection as a substitute for branch-circuit overcurrent devices.

records.prompt: The largest size grounding electrode conductor to a concrete-encased electrode is not required to be larger than ___ copper.
records.gist: A grounding electrode conductor that runs only to a concrete-encased electrode has a size cap, no matter how big the service is. The question asks the largest copper size ever required there.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: grounding electrode. Start with 250.66(B), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three jobs, three parts. Grounding connects the system to the earth (rods, plates, concrete-encased electrodes) to drain lightning and surges. Bonding joins all the metal parts together so fault current has a fast low-resistance road back to the source that trips the breaker. The grounded conductor (neutral, white) carries normal current; the grounding conductor (green/bare) carries only fault current. The main bonding jumper is where neutral and ground meet — at the service, and only there.

This asks you to name the grounding or bonding part in this installation. Subject: grounding electrode. Trace the fault-current path: what connects the equipment back to the source?

LOOKUP FOCUS

If the grounding electrode conductor or bonding jumper connected to a single or multiple concrete-encased electrode(s), as described in 250.52(A)(3), does not extend on to other types of electrodes that require a larger size of conductor, the grounding electrode conductor shall not be required to be larger than 4 AWG copper wire.

WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
A GFCI watches the current going out and coming back on a circuit. If even a tiny amount leaks — say, through a person to ground — it trips in a fraction of a second. That is why the NEC demands GFCI protection anywhere water and electricity can meet: bathrooms, kitchens, garages, outdoors, crawl spaces, laundry areas, pools, and spas.

Article 100 Definitions — Coordination, Selective
Coordination, Selective. (Selective Coordination) Localization of an overcurrent condition to restrict outages to the circuit or equipment affected, accomplished by the selection and installation of overcurrent protective devices and their ratings or settings for the full range of available overcurrents, from overload to the available fault current, and for the full range of overcurrent protective device opening times associated with those overcurrents. (CMP—10)

Article 100 defines selective coordination as localizing an overcurrent to the affected circuit. Not A: An arc-fault circuit interrupter detects arcing faults; it does not localize outages between devices. Not B: Overload protection guards against sustained excess current; it is not the defined localization term. Not D: Selective coordination is the defined term, so none of these is incorrect.

records.prompt: Torque requirements for motor control circuit device terminals must be a minimum of ___ lbs-inch (unless otherwise identified) for screw-type pressure terminals used for #14 and smaller copper conductors.

records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
A motor circuit has two separate protections doing two jobs. The overload device (heaters, overload relay) guards against a motor slowly cooking from too much load — sized from the motor's own nameplate amps (125% for sturdy motors, 115% for the rest), with one overload unit per phase (three units on a three-phase motor). The breaker or fuses handle violent short circuits and ground faults. The controller starts and stops the motor; the disconnect within sight of the motor lets a worker be sure it cannot restart while hands are on it.

records.prompt: The power in a circuit is 2 W and the voltage is 20 VDC. What is the circuit current?
records.gist: Power equals voltage times current, so current is power divided by voltage. The question gives watts and volts and asks for the current.
keywords: identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: identify the equipment, location, and requirement. Start with General calculation, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three formulas run the math questions. Ohm's law: volts = amps × ohms. Power: watts = volts × amps (so amps = watts ÷ volts). Resistors in parallel combine as the product over the sum. Voltage drop percent is volts lost ÷ source volts. And AC frequency: 60 cycles per second means one full 360° wave takes 1/60 s. To turn a percent into a fraction, write it over 100 and reduce.

In plain terms, the question is: "The power in a circuit is 2 W and the voltage is 20 VDC. What is the circuit current?" Break it into pieces — what equipment, what location or measurement, and what the NEC must say about it — then find the choice that satisfies every piece.

LOOKUP FOCUS
identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.reference_text:
Electrical Theory • Power Equation (Watt's Law)
Power equals voltage times current (P = E × I). Rearranged for current, I = P ÷ E: divide the power in watts by the voltage in volts to get the current in amperes.
records.tip_short: Current equals power divided by voltage (I = P / E), so 2 watts over 20 volts is one tenth of an ampere. Correct: A — 0.10 A. I = P / E = 2 watts / 20 volts = 0.10 amperes. Not B: 0.20 amperes would require 4 watts at 20 volts; 2 watts at 20 volts is 0.10 amperes. Not C: 0.30 amperes would be 6 watts at 20 volts, three times the stated power. Not D: 0.40 amperes would be 8 watts at 20 volts, four times the stated 2 watts.
records.formula: Ohm's power law: amps = watts ÷ volts.
choice_notes: I = P / E = 2 watts / 20 volts = 0.10 amperes.
0.20 amperes would require 4 watts at 20 volts; 2 watts at 20 volts is 0.10 amperes.
0.30 amperes would be 6 watts at 20 volts, three times the stated power.

records.prompt: The motor branch-circuit short-circuit and ground-fault protective device must be capable of carrying the ___ current of the motor.

Delicate internals — luminaire ballasts, appliance circuits, control wiring — get smaller supplementary protectors, but those never replace branch-circuit protection. Where staying online matters, selective coordination stages the devices so only the faulted circuit goes dark.
