records.prompt: The ampacity for the supply conductors for a resistance welder with a duty cycle of 15% and a primary current of 21 amps is ___.
records.gist: Resistance welder supply conductors are sized from the primary current times a multiplier from the duty-cycle table. The question gives a 15 percent duty cycle and 21 amps and asks the resulting ampacity.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: ampacity, conductors. Start with Table 630.31(A), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three formulas run the math questions. Ohm's law: volts = amps × ohms. Power: watts = volts × amps (so amps = watts ÷ volts). Resistors in parallel combine as the product over the sum. Voltage drop percent is volts lost ÷ source volts. And AC frequency: 60 cycles per second means one full 360° wave takes 1/60 s. To turn a percent into a fraction, write it over 100 and reduce.

This asks how many amps the conductor may safely carry under the stated conditions. Subject: welder. Numbers in the question: 15%, 21 amps. Apply temperature and adjustment factors first, then read the resulting ampacity.

LOOKUP FOCUS
ampacity, conductors
records.reference_text:
630.31(A) Individual Welders
The ampacity of conductors for individual welders shall comply with the following:
(2) The ampacity of the supply conductors for a welder wired for a specific operation for which the actual primary current and duty cycle are known and remain unchanged shall not be less than the product of the actual primary current and the multiplier specified in Table 630.31(A) for the duty cycle at which the welder will be operated.
Table 630.31(A) Duty Cycle Multiplication Factors for Resistance Welders
Duty Cycle (%)	Multiplier
50	0.71
40	0.63
30	0.55
25	0.50
20	0.45
15	0.39
10	0.32
7.5	0.27
5 or less	0.22
reference_table: NOTE: Supply-conductor ampacity = actual primary current × the multiplier for the duty cycle.
records.tip_short: Resistance welder supply ampacity: primary current times the duty-cycle factor; 15 percent uses 0.39. Correct: B — 8.19 amps. Table 630.31(A) factor for 15 percent duty cycle is 0.39: 21 × 0.39 = 8.19 amperes. Not A: 9.45 amperes uses the 20 percent factor of 0.45, not the 15 percent factor. Not C: 11.2 amperes does not match the 0.39 factor for a 15 percent duty cycle. Not D: 21 amperes ignores the duty-cycle multiplication factor required by 630.31(A).
records.formula: Multiply the actual primary current by the Table 630.31(A) multiplier for the duty cycle (each multiplier is the square root of the duty cycle, rounded).
choice_notes: 9.45 amperes uses the 20 percent factor of 0.45, not the 15 percent factor.
Table 630.31(A) factor for 15 percent duty cycle is 0.39: 21 × 0.39 = 8.19 amperes.
11.2 amperes does not match the 0.39 factor for a 15 percent duty cycle.

records.prompt: A circuit contains two 2,000 ohm resistors connected in parallel. What is the total resistance of the circuit?

records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three formulas run the math questions. Ohm's law: volts = amps × ohms. Power: watts = volts × amps (so amps = watts ÷ volts). Resistors in parallel combine as the product over the sum. Voltage drop percent is volts lost ÷ source volts. And AC frequency: 60 cycles per second means one full 360° wave takes 1/60 s. To turn a percent into a fraction, write it over 100 and reduce.

records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three formulas run the math questions. Ohm's law: volts = amps × ohms. Power: watts = volts × amps (so amps = watts ÷ volts). Resistors in parallel combine as the product over the sum. records.prompt: #2/0 THW copper service conductors would require a grounding electrode conductor of ___.

records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: grounding electrode, conductors. Start with Table 250.66, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three jobs, three parts. Grounding connects the system to the earth (rods, plates, concrete-encased electrodes) to drain lightning and surges. Bonding joins all the metal parts together so fault current has a fast low-resistance road back to the source that trips the breaker. The grounded conductor (neutral, white) carries normal current; the grounding conductor (green/bare) carries only fault current. The main bonding jumper is where neutral and ground meet — at the service, and only there.

records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: motor, load calculation. Start with 430.32(C), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
A motor circuit has two separate protections doing two jobs. The overload device (heaters, overload relay) guards against a motor slowly cooking from too much load — sized from the motor's own nameplate amps (125% for sturdy motors, 115% for the rest), with one overload unit per phase (three units on a three-phase motor). The breaker or fuses handle violent short circuits and ground faults. The controller starts and stops the motor; the disconnect within sight of the motor lets a worker be sure it cannot restart while hands are on it.

This is a maximum-limit question. Subject: motor. Numbers in the question: 2 hp, 24 amps. The correct choice is the maximum value the NEC allows — eliminate any choice on the wrong side of that limit.

LOOKUP FOCUS
motor, load calculation
records.reference_text:
430.32 Continuous-Duty Motors
(C) Selection of Overload Device
Where the sensing element or setting or sizing of the overload device selected in accordance with 430.32(A)(1) and 430.32(B)(1) is not sufficient to start the motor or to carry the load, higher size sensing elements or incremental settings or sizing shall be permitted to be used, provided the trip current of the overload device does not exceed the following percentage of motor nameplate full-load current rating:
Motors with marked service factor 1.15 or greater	140%
Motors with a marked temperature rise 40°C or less	140%
All other motors	130%
records.tip_short: Maximum overload (430.32(C)): 140 percent for a marked service factor of 1.15 or more or a temperature rise of 40 degrees C or less; 130 percent for all other motors. Correct: D — 33.6.
records.formula: Full-load current × the 430.32(C) maximum percentage for the motor's service factor.
choice_notes: 24 amperes is the full-load current itself, with no allowance.
27.6 amperes is 115 percent, the normal 430.32(A)(1) setting for this motor, not the maximum.
31.2 amperes is 130 percent, for motors without the qualifying service factor.
Service factor 1.2 is 1.15 or greater, so 140 percent applies: 24 x 1.40 = 33.6 amperes.

records.prompt: What is the cubic inch capacity required for a device box containing one duplex receptacle, cable clamps and two #12-2 with ground nonmetallic sheathed cables (romex)?
records.gist: Box fill counts conductors, plus extra allowances for devices, clamps, and grounding conductors, all based on the largest conductor. The question asks the total for this receptacle box.
records.article_title: Outlet, Device, Pull, and Junction Boxes; Conduit Bodies; Fittings; and Handhole Enclosures
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: receptacle outlet, cable, box / enclosure. Start with 314.16(B), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Boxes are sized by volume, not vibes: every wire, clamp, and device yoke eats cubic inches, so a crowded box is a Code violation and a fire risk. Device boxes need minimum depth (a flush device needs room behind it), and unused breaker or knockout openings must be closed with listed fillers so fingers and sparks can't get in. Switchboards and panelboards add their own rules: conductors belong only in the section they terminate in, and rear-access gear must say so on the front.

This asks for the receptacle rule in this spot. Subject: receptacle. Decide whether the question wants a location, a height, a count, or a protection requirement, then match that to the rule.

LOOKUP FOCUS
receptacle outlet, cable, box / enclosure
records.reference_text:
314.16 Number of Conductors in Outlet, Device, and Junction Boxes, and Conduit Bodies
(B) Box Fill Calculations
(2) Clamp Fill
Where one or more internal cable clamps, whether factory or field supplied, are present in the box, a single volume allowance in accordance with Table 314.16(B)(1) shall be made based on the largest conductor present in the box. No allowance shall be required for a cable connector with its clamping mechanism outside the box.
(4) Device or Equipment Fill
For each yoke or strap containing one or more devices or equipment, a double volume allowance in accordance with Table 314.16(B)(1) shall be made for each yoke or strap based on the largest conductor connected to a device(s) or equipment supported by that yoke or strap. A device or utilization equipment wider than a single 50 mm (2 in.) device box as described in Table 314.16(A) shall have double volume allowances provided for each gang required for mounting.
(5) Equipment Grounding Conductor Fill
Where up to four equipment grounding conductors enter a box, a single volume allowance in accordance with Table 314.16(B)(1) shall be made based on the largest equipment grounding conductor entering the box. A 1/4 volume allowance shall be made for each additional equipment grounding conductor that enters the box, based on the largest equipment grounding conductor entering the box.
Table 314.16(B)(1) Volume Allowance Required per Conductor
Size of Conductor (AWG)	Free Space Within Box for Each Conductor
12	36.9	2.25
records.tip_short: Box fill (314.16(B)): each conductor one allowance; clamps one; each device yoke two; all equipment grounding conductors (up to four) one; sized by the largest conductor. Correct: D — 18 cu.in. 4 conductors + 2 for the receptacle + 1 for clamps + 1 for the grounds = 8 x 2.25 = 18 cubic inches. Not A: 13.5 cubic inches leaves out allowances; four conductors plus device, clamps, and grounds total 18. Not B: 15.75 cubic inches misses one allowance; the full count is eight allowances of 2.25. Not C: 16 cubic inches does not match the 2.25 cubic inch allowances for #12 conductors.
records.formula: Count allowances (conductors, clamps, device yoke x 2, grounds) and multiply by the Table 314.16(B)(1) volume for the largest conductor.
choice_notes: 13.5 cubic inches leaves out allowances; four conductors plus device, clamps, and grounds total 18.
15.75 cubic inches misses one allowance; the full count is eight allowances of 2.25.
16 cubic inches does not match the 2.25 cubic inch allowances for #12 conductors.

records.prompt: There are seven current carrying #12 THHN conductors run in a conduit where the ambient temperature is 30°C. What is the ampacity of each conductor?
records.gist: Bundling more than three current-carrying conductors traps heat, so each one is derated. The question asks the adjusted ampacity of THHN wire in this group.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: ampacity, conduit, conductors. Start with Table 310.15(C)(1), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Decode the letters first: EMT = Electrical Metallic Tubing (thin-wall, hand-bendable). RMC = Rigid Metal Conduit (thick threaded steel). IMC = Intermediate (in between). FMC = Flexible Metal Conduit (bendable whip). ENT = Electrical Nonmetallic Tubing (blue smurf tube). LFMC = Liquidtight Flexible Metal (sealed whip). RNC = Rigid Nonmetallic Conduit (PVC). Rules answer three things: clearance from wood framing (1-1/4 in. or a nail plate), burial depth, and strapping (within a foot of every box, then every few feet by type).

This asks how many amps the conductor may safely carry under the stated conditions. Subject: conduit. Apply temperature and adjustment factors first, then read the resulting ampacity.

records.prompt: A 10 unit apartment building has a 4.5 kW water heater in each unit. What is the demand on the service for these water heaters? Use standard method of calculation.

records.article_title: Branch-Circuit, Feeder, and Service Load Calculations
keywords: identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: identify the equipment, location, and requirement. Start with 220.53, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Load calculations never just add everything up, because a home never runs all loads at once. Start with 3 VA per square foot of living space (outside dimensions, minus open porches and unfinished spaces), add 1,500 VA for each small-appliance and laundry circuit, then shrink the subtotal with the demand factor (first 3,000 VA at full value, 3,001 to 120,000 VA at 35%, the remainder at 25%). Ranges and dryers use their own tables — a range nameplate is only the starting point. Heat and AC: count the larger one, never both.

In plain terms, the question is: "A 10 unit apartment building has a 4.5 kW water heater in each unit. What is the demand on the service for these water heaters? Use…" Break it into pieces — what equipment, what location or measurement, and what the NEC must say about it — then find the choice that satisfies every piece.

LOOKUP FOCUS
identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.reference_text:
220.53 Appliance Load - Dwelling Unit(s)
Applying a demand factor of 75 percent to the nameplate rating load of four or more appliances rated 1/4 hp or greater, or 500 watts or greater, that are fastened in place, and that are served by the same feeder or service in a one-family, two-family, or multifamily dwelling shall be permitted. This demand factor shall not apply to the following:
records.tip_short: Fastened-in-place appliances (220.53): 75 percent for four or more, excluding cooking equipment, dryers, space heating, air conditioning, and EVSE, which have their own rules. Correct: C — 33.75 kW.
records.formula: Total nameplate load × 75% (220.53, four or more appliances).
choice_notes: 45 kW is the connected load with no demand factor; ten appliances qualify for 75 percent.
50 kW is more than the connected load of 45 kW.
10 x 4.5 kW = 45 kW; four or more appliances take 75 percent; 45 x 0.75 = 33.75 kW.
36 kW applies 80 percent; 220.53 uses 75 percent.

records.prompt: The overcurrent protection for a #10 RHH conductor in a conduit at 104°F is ___ amps.
records.gist: A small conductor's overcurrent protection is capped by a separate rule no matter how high its corrected ampacity is. The question asks the protection for this 90 degree C wire.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: overcurrent protection, conduit. Start with 240.4(D), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Overcurrent protection works in layers. The branch breaker or fuse handles violent short circuits and ground faults and must carry the motor's starting surge without tripping. Delicate internals — luminaire ballasts, appliance circuits, control wiring — get smaller supplementary protectors, but those never replace branch-circuit protection. Where staying online matters, selective coordination stages the devices so only the faulted circuit goes dark.

This asks which wiring-method rule fits this installation. Subject: conduit. Focus on whether the question is about support spacing, fill, burial cover, protection from damage, or where the method is permitted.

LOOKUP FOCUS
overcurrent protection, conduit
records.reference_text:
240.4 Protection of Conductors
(D) Small Conductors
Unless specifically permitted in 240.4(E) or (G), the overcurrent protection shall not exceed that required by 240.4(D)(1) through (D)(8) after any correction factors for ambient temperature and number of conductors have been applied.
(8) 10 AWG Copper
30 amperes
records.tip_short: Small conductors (240.4(D)): 14 AWG copper 15 A, 12 AWG 20 A, 10 AWG 30 A, whatever the ampacity after correction, unless 240.4(E) or (G) applies. Correct: A — 30.
records.formula: Correct the ampacity, then apply the 240.4(D) limit for the conductor size.
records.worked: 40 A × 0.91 = 36.4 A ampacity; 240.4(D)(8) limits 10 AWG copper to 30 A.
choice_notes: 240.4(D)(8) limits 10 AWG copper to 30 amperes of overcurrent protection, even though its corrected ampacity is 36.4 amperes.
36.4 amperes is the corrected ampacity (40 x 0.91); 240.4(D) caps the protection at 30 amperes.
40 amperes is the uncorrected 90 degree C ampacity; 240.4(D) caps 10 AWG copper at 30 amperes.
20 amperes is the limit for 12 AWG copper, not 10 AWG.

records.prompt: The total load of a 15 hp, 208v, three-phase induction motor is closest to ___ va.

records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
A motor circuit has two separate protections doing two jobs. The overload device (heaters, overload relay) guards against a motor slowly cooking from too much load — sized from the motor's own nameplate amps (125% for sturdy motors, 115% for the rest), with one overload unit per phase (three units on a three-phase motor). The breaker or fuses handle violent short circuits and ground faults. The controller starts and stops the motor; the disconnect within sight of the motor lets a worker be sure it cannot restart while hands are on it.

records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: cable. Start with NEC 334.116(B), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three formulas run the math questions. Ohm's law: volts = amps × ohms. Power: watts = volts × amps (so amps = watts ÷ volts). Resistors in parallel combine as the product over the sum. Voltage drop percent is volts lost ÷ source volts. And AC frequency: 60 cycles per second means one full 360° wave takes 1/60 s. To turn a percent into a fraction, write it over 100 and reduce.

records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: conduit. Start with 358.14, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Boxes are sized by volume, not vibes: every wire, clamp, and device yoke eats cubic inches, so a crowded box is a Code violation and a fire risk. Device boxes need minimum depth (a flush device needs room behind it), and unused breaker or knockout openings must be closed with listed fillers so fingers and sparks can't get in. Switchboards and panelboards add their own rules: conductors belong only in the section they terminate in, and rear-access gear must say so on the front.

In plain terms, the question is: "Aluminum fittings and enclosures shall be permitted to be used with ___." Break it into pieces — what equipment, what location or measurement, and what the NEC must say about it — then find the choice that satisfies every piece.

records.reference_text:
358.14 Dissimilar Metals
Where practicable, dissimilar metals in contact anywhere in the system shall be avoided to eliminate the possibility of galvanic action.
Stainless steel and aluminum fittings and enclosures shall be permitted to be used with galvanized steel EMT, and galvanized steel fittings and enclosures shall be permitted to be used with aluminum EMT where not subject to severe corrosive influences.

records.prompt: The number of conductors allowed in LFNC must not exceed that permitted by the percentage fill specified in ___, Chapter 9.

records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three formulas run the math questions. Ohm's law: volts = amps × ohms. Power: watts = volts × amps (so amps = watts ÷ volts). Resistors in parallel combine as the product over the sum. Voltage drop percent is volts lost ÷ source volts. And AC frequency: 60 cycles per second means one full 360° wave takes 1/60 s. To turn a percent into a fraction, write it over 100 and reduce.

records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three jobs, three parts. Grounding connects the system to the earth (rods, plates, concrete-encased electrodes) to drain lightning and surges. Bonding joins all the metal parts together so fault current has a fast low-resistance road back to the source that trips the breaker. The grounded conductor (neutral, white) carries normal current; the grounding conductor (green/bare) carries only fault current. The main bonding jumper is where neutral and ground meet — at the service, and only there.

Load calculations never just add everything up, because a home never runs all loads at once. A GFCI watches the current going out and coming back on a circuit. If even a tiny amount leaks — say, through a person to ground — it trips in a fraction of a second. (2) Indoor Equipment Requiring Dedicated Equipment Spaces

Three formulas run the math questions. Ohm's law: volts = amps × ohms. Power: watts = volts × amps (so amps = watts ÷ volts). Resistors in parallel combine as the product over the sum. 220.14(H) Fixed Multioutlet Assemblies
Fixed multioutlet assemblies used in other than dwelling units or the guest rooms or guest suites of hotels or motels shall be calculated in accordance with the following:
(1) Where appliances are unlikely to be used simultaneously, each 1.5 m (5 ft) or fraction thereof of each separate and continuous length shall be considered as one outlet of not less than 180 volt-amperes.
(2) Where appliances are likely to be used simultaneously, each 300 mm (1 ft) or fraction thereof shall be considered as an outlet of not less than 180 volt-amperes.

records.formula: Not used simultaneously: count one 180 VA outlet for each 5 ft or fraction of the assembly (220.14(H)(1)), then multiply.

records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Overcurrent protection works in layers. The branch breaker or fuse handles violent short circuits and ground faults and must carry the motor's starting surge without tripping. Delicate internals — luminaire ballasts, appliance circuits, control wiring — get smaller supplementary protectors, but those never replace branch-circuit protection. Where staying online matters, selective coordination stages the devices so only the faulted circuit goes dark.

records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
A motor circuit has two separate protections doing two jobs. The overload device (heaters, overload relay) guards against a motor slowly cooking from too much load — sized from the motor's own nameplate amps (125% for sturdy motors, 115% for the rest), with one overload unit per phase (three units on a three-phase motor). The breaker or fuses handle violent short circuits and ground faults. The controller starts and stops the motor; the disconnect within sight of the motor lets a worker be sure it cannot restart while hands are on it.

424.20(A) Serving as Both Controllers and Disconnecting Means
Thermostatically controlled switching devices and combination thermostats and manually controlled switches shall be permitted to serve as both controllers and disconnecting means, provided they meet all of the following conditions:

(2) Directly open all ungrounded conductors when manually placed in the "off" position

records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three jobs, three parts. Grounding connects the system to the earth (rods, plates, concrete-encased electrodes) to drain lightning and surges. Bonding joins all the metal parts together so fault current has a fast low-resistance road back to the source that trips the breaker. The grounded conductor (neutral, white) carries normal current; the grounding conductor (green/bare) carries only fault current. The main bonding jumper is where neutral and ground meet — at the service, and only there.

Type UF cable shall be permitted as follows:
(1) For use underground, including direct burial in the earth.

records.prompt: One or more metal in-ground support structures in direct contact with the earth vertically for ___ feet or more, with or without concrete encasement, is a permitted grounding electrode.

records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three jobs, three parts. Grounding connects the system to the earth (rods, plates, concrete-encased electrodes) to drain lightning and surges. Bonding joins all the metal parts together so fault current has a fast low-resistance road back to the source that trips the breaker. The grounded conductor (neutral, white) carries normal current; the grounding conductor (green/bare) carries only fault current. The main bonding jumper is where neutral and ground meet — at the service, and only there.

records.prompt: Which of the following is a flexible cord type that is permitted in a wet location and is sunlight resistant?
records.gist: Flexible cord type letters tell where a cord may be used. The question asks which one of these four types is a flexible cord rated for wet locations that is also sunlight resistant.

records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: identify the equipment, location, and requirement. Start with Table 400.4 and Note 9, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Flexible cords are temporary wiring, not a substitute for fixed circuits — they must stay continuous (no splices except repairing hard-service cord), stay short, and match the job's toughness: junior hard-service (SJ) for light duty, hard-service (S, ST) for tools and appliances. The letters on a cord are a code: S = hard service, J = junior hard service (300 V), T = thermoplastic, O = oil-resistant jacket, OO = oil-resistant jacket and insulation, W = wet locations and sunlight resistant. Building wires such as THWN and XHWN also carry a W (wet location), but they are single conductors for raceways, not flexible cords, and Table 400.4 does not list them.

In plain terms, the question is: "Which of the following is a flexible cord type that is permitted in a wet location and is sunlight resistant?"

Read the situation, then test each choice against it. Eliminate choices that contradict the stated conditions; the survivor that fits all of them is the answer.

LOOKUP FOCUS
identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.reference_text:
Table 400.4 Flexible Cords and Flexible Cables, Note 9
Cords that comply with the requirements for outdoor cords and are so listed shall be permitted to be designated as weather and water resistant with the suffix "W" after the Code type designation. Cords with the "W" suffix are suitable for use in wet locations and are sunlight resistant.
reference_table: NOTE: Table 400.4 Note 9: cords with the "W" suffix are suitable for use in wet locations and are sunlight resistant. THWN and XHWN are building wires, not flexible cords.

No W on a cord means no wet rating. Correct: B — STOOW. STOOW reads S = hard-service cord, T = thermoplastic, OO = oil-resistant insulation and jacket, W = wet locations and sunlight. Table 400.4 lists it for damp and wet locations, and Note 9 says every W cord is sunlight resistant. Not A: SPT-2 is light-duty parallel lamp cord (the flat two-wire kind). Table 400.4 lists it for damp locations only, and it has no W. The same cord with a W, SPT-2W, is rated for wet locations, but SPT-2W is not a choice here. Not C: THWN is a single building wire for dry and wet locations (Table 310.4(1)), pulled in a raceway. It is not a flexible cord, so Table 400.4 does not list it. Not D: XHWN is a single building wire for dry and wet locations (Table 310.4(1)), pulled in a raceway. It is not a flexible cord, so Table 400.4 does not list it.

records.prompt: Grounded conductors of circuits with parallel conductors in a panelboard shall be permitted to terminate in a single terminal if the terminal is ___ for connection of more than one conductor.

records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three jobs, three parts. Grounding connects the system to the earth (rods, plates, concrete-encased electrodes) to drain lightning and surges. Bonding joins all the metal parts together so fault current has a fast low-resistance road back to the source that trips the breaker. The grounded conductor (neutral, white) carries normal current; the grounding conductor (green/bare) carries only fault current. The main bonding jumper is where neutral and ground meet — at the service, and only there.

records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three formulas run the math questions. Ohm's law: volts = amps × ohms. Power: watts = volts × amps (so amps = watts ÷ volts). Resistors in parallel combine as the product over the sum. records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: motor, disconnecting means. Start with 430.102(B)(2), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
A motor circuit has two separate protections doing two jobs. The overload device (heaters, overload relay) guards against a motor slowly cooking from too much load — sized from the motor's own nameplate amps (125% for sturdy motors, 115% for the rest), with one overload unit per phase (three units on a three-phase motor). The breaker or fuses handle violent short circuits and ground faults. The controller starts and stops the motor; the disconnect within sight of the motor lets a worker be sure it cannot restart while hands are on it.

records.reference_text:
430.102(B)(2) Motor Controller Disconnect
The motor controller disconnecting means required in accordance with 430.102(A) shall be permitted to serve as the disconnecting means for the motor if it is in sight from the motor location and the driven machinery location.
Exception to (1) and (2): The disconnecting means for the motor shall not be required under either of the following conditions if the motor controller disconnecting means required in 430.102(A) is lockable in accordance with 110.25:
(1) Where such a location of the disconnecting means for the motor is impracticable or introduces additional or increased hazards to persons or property
(2) In industrial installations, with written safety procedures, where conditions of maintenance and supervision ensure that only qualified persons service the equipment

Not A: Moving the driven machinery is not a Code remedy; the 430.102(B) Exception requires the controller disconnect to be lockable. Not C: Accessibility alone does not protect a worker at a motor out of sight; the 430.102(B) Exception requires a lockable disconnect. Not D: An isolating switch is not required here; the 430.102(B) Exception requires the controller disconnect to be lockable open.

Electrical equipment, such as switchboards, switchgear, enclosed panelboards, industrial control panels, meter socket enclosures, and motor control centers, that is in other than dwelling units, and is likely to require examination, adjustment, servicing, or maintenance while energized, shall be field or factory marked to warn qualified persons of potential electric arc flash hazards. The marking shall meet the requirements in 110.21(B) and shall be located so as to be clearly visible to qualified persons before examination, adjustment, servicing, or maintenance of the equipment.
records.tip_short: Arc flash warning labels are required on serviceable gear everywhere except dwelling units, per 110.16(A). Correct: D — dwelling units. 110.16(A) applies to equipment in other than dwelling units, so homes are exempt. Not A: Locked rooms are not exempt; 110.16(A) exempts only dwelling units. Not B: Schools are not exempt; equipment there still needs arc flash hazard marking. Not C: Testing areas are not exempt; 110.16(A) exempts only dwelling units.
choice_notes: Locked rooms are not exempt; 110.16(A) exempts only dwelling units.
Schools are not exempt; equipment there still needs arc flash hazard marking.

records.prompt: Feeders supplying two or more branch circuits for diagnostic imaging and treatment equipment shall have an ampacity of not less than 50 percent of the ___ demand rating of the largest unit, plus 25 percent of that rating for the next largest unit, plus 10 percent for each additional unit.
records.gist: Diagnostic imaging equipment draws brief high-current pulses, so its feeders follow the pulse-based rating rather than the continuous one. The question asks which demand rating that is.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: overcurrent protection, conductors. Start with 517.73(B), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Overcurrent protection works in layers. The branch breaker or fuse handles violent short circuits and ground faults and must carry the motor's starting surge without tripping. Delicate internals — luminaire ballasts, appliance circuits, control wiring — get smaller supplementary protectors, but those never replace branch-circuit protection. Where staying online matters, selective coordination stages the devices so only the faulted circuit goes dark.

This is a minimum-limit question. Subject: feeder. Numbers in the question: 50 percent, 25 percent, 10 percent. The correct choice is the minimum value the NEC allows — eliminate any choice on the wrong side of that limit.

LOOKUP FOCUS
overcurrent protection, conductors
records.reference_text:
517.73(B) Feeders
The ampacity of supply feeders and the current rating of overcurrent protective devices supplying two or more branch circuits supplying diagnostic imaging and treatment equipment shall not be less than 50 percent of the momentary demand rating of the largest unit, plus 25 percent of the momentary demand rating of the next largest unit, plus 10 percent of the momentary demand rating of each additional unit.

Not A: Continuous is not a rating term used for X-ray equipment in 517.73. Not B: Non-continuous is not an X-ray rating term in 517.73. Not C: Instantaneous is not the Code term; 517.73 bases ratings on the momentary rating.

records.prompt: Flexible cord used in extension cords made with separately listed and installed components shall be permitted to be supplied by a branch circuit in accordance with the following: 20 ampere circuits ___ and larger.

records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Flexible cords are temporary wiring, not a substitute for fixed circuits — they must stay continuous (no splices except repairing hard-service cord), stay short, and match the job's toughness: junior hard-service (SJ) for light duty, hard-service (S, ST) for tools and appliances, extra-hard (SO) for construction sites. records.reference_text:
708.54 Selective Coordination
(B) Replacements
Where critical operations power system(s) OCPDs are replaced, they shall be reevaluated to ensure selective coordination is maintained with all supply-side and load-side OCPDs.
(C) Modifications
If modifications, additions, or deletions to the critical operations power system(s) occur, selective coordination of the critical operations power system(s) OCPDs with all supply-side and load-side OCPDs shall be reevaluated.
Exception: Selective coordination shall not be required between two overcurrent devices located in series if no loads are connected in parallel with the downstream device.

records.prompt: Electrical equipment provided with ___ openings shall be installed so that walls or other obstructions do not prevent the free circulation of air through the equipment.
records.gist: Ventilated equipment requires unobstructed airflow. The question asks what kind of openings trigger that rule.
keywords: identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: identify the equipment, location, and requirement. Start with 110.13(B), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Working space is the empty bubble an electrician stands in while servicing live gear — nobody may store boxes or park equipment in it. The NEC measures it three ways: depth in front (3+ ft depending on voltage and what faces the gear — concrete or brick walls facing you mean deeper space), 30 in. minimum width (or the equipment's width), and 6-1/2 ft of headroom. Big gear needs doors that swing 90° and a way out that open doors can't block. Above panels, the space up to the ceiling belongs to electrics only — no pipes or ducts.

In plain terms, the question is: "Electrical equipment provided with ___ openings shall be installed so that walls or other obstructions do not prevent the free circulation…" Break it into pieces — what equipment, what location or measurement, and what the NEC must say about it — then find the choice that satisfies every piece.

records.reference_text:
110.13(B) Cooling
Electrical equipment that depends on the natural circulation of air and convection principles for cooling of exposed surfaces shall be installed so that room airflow over such surfaces is not prevented by walls or by adjacent installed equipment. For equipment designed for floor mounting, clearance between top surfaces and adjacent surfaces shall be provided to dissipate rising warm air.
Electrical equipment provided with ventilating openings shall be installed so that walls or other obstructions do not prevent the free circulation of air through the equipment.
records.tip_short: Never block the vents: equipment with ventilating openings needs free airflow through it, per 110.13(B). Correct: A — ventilating. 110.13(B) says equipment provided with ventilating openings must allow free circulation of air. Not B: Vented is close in meaning but not the Code term; 110.13(B) says ventilating openings. Not C: Filtered openings are not the subject of 110.13(B). Not D: Gated openings are not mentioned in 110.13(B).

records.prompt: The feeder or branch circuit disconnecting means shall have a rating not less than the ___ load to be served.
records.gist: Service equipment must be rated not less than the total computed load. The question asks which load value sets its minimum size.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: branch circuit, feeder, load calculation, disconnecting means. Start with 225.39, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Branch circuits are rated by their breaker: the standard sizes are 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, and 50 amps. A multiwire (shared-neutral) circuit must open all its ungrounded legs together so no leg can stay live alone. And the number of circuits in a building comes from the total load divided by circuit size — fractional results always round up, because half a circuit doesn't exist.

This is a minimum-limit question. Subject: disconnecting means. The correct choice is the minimum value the NEC allows — eliminate any choice on the wrong side of that limit.

LOOKUP FOCUS
branch circuit, feeder, load calculation, disconnecting means
records.reference_text:
225.39 Rating of Disconnect
The feeder or branch-circuit disconnecting means shall have a rating of not less than the calculated load to be supplied, determined in accordance with Parts I and II of Article 220 for branch circuits, Part III or IV of Article 220 for feeders, or Part V of Article 220 for farm loads. Where the branch circuit or feeder disconnecting means consists of more than one switch or circuit breaker, as permitted by 225.33, combining the ratings of all the switches or circuit breakers for determining the rating of the disconnecting means shall be permitted. In no case shall the rating be lower than specified in 225.39(A), (B), (C), or (D).
(A) One-Circuit Installation
For installations to supply only limited loads of a single branch circuit, the branch circuit disconnecting means shall have a rating of not less than 15 amperes.
records.tip_short: Outside feeder or branch circuit disconnects must be rated at least the calculated load from Article 220. Correct: C — calculated. 225.39 requires a rating not less than the calculated load to be supplied. Not A: Actual load is not the basis; 225.39 uses the load calculated under Article 220. Not B: Minimum load is not the basis; the rating must not be less than the calculated load. Not D: Maximum load is not the Code basis; 225.39 uses the calculated load.

Minimum load is not the basis; the rating must not be less than the calculated load.

WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS

Appliances play by cord-and-plug rules: a kitchen disposer may use a short flexible cord (18 in. to 3 ft) instead of hard wiring, and a room air conditioner gets a short cord matched to its voltage (about 10 ft at 120 V, 6 ft at 240 V). 424.36 Clearances of Wiring in Ceilings
Wiring located above heated ceilings shall be spaced not less than 50 mm (2 in.) above the heated ceiling. The ampacity of conductors shall be calculated on the basis of an assumed ambient temperature of not less than 50°C (122°F), applying the correction factors in accordance with 310.15(B)(1). If this wiring is located above thermal insulation having a minimum thickness of 50 mm (2 in.), it shall be subject to the ambient correction in accordance with 310.15(B)(1).

records.prompt: The temperature correction and adjustment factors shall be permitted to be applied to the ampacity for the temperature rating of the conductor, if the corrected and adjusted ampacity does not exceed the ampacity for the temperature rating of the ___ in accordance with the provisions of 110.14(C).
records.gist: Conductors may start from their own temperature rating, but the lowest temperature rating in the chain caps the final ampacity. The question asks what that link is called.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: ampacity. Start with 310.15(A), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Load calculations never just add everything up, because a home never runs all loads at once. Start with 3 VA per square foot of living space (outside dimensions, minus open porches and unfinished spaces), add 1,500 VA for each small-appliance and laundry circuit, then shrink the subtotal with the demand factor (first 3,000 VA at full value, 3,001 to 120,000 VA at 35%, the remainder at 25%). Ranges and dryers use their own tables — a range nameplate is only the starting point. Heat and AC: count the larger one, never both.

This asks how many amps the conductor may safely carry under the stated conditions. Apply temperature and adjustment factors first, then read the resulting ampacity.

LOOKUP FOCUS
ampacity
records.reference_text:
310.15(A) General
Ampacities for conductors rated 0 volts to 2000 volts shall be as specified in the Ampacity Table 310.16 through Table 310.21, as modified by 310.15(A) through (F) and 310.12. Under engineering supervision, ampacities of sizes not shown in ampacity tables for conductors meeting the general wiring requirements shall be permitted to be determined by interpolation of the adjacent conductors based on the conductor's circular-mil area.
The temperature correction and adjustment factors shall be permitted to be applied to the ampacity for the temperature rating of the conductor, if the corrected and adjusted ampacity does not exceed the ampacity for the temperature rating of the termination in accordance with 110.14(C).

records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: identify the equipment, location, and requirement. Start with 700.7(A), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Emergency systems must work when normal power doesn't: fire-pump controllers and parts sit high and dry above floors, the emergency source gets marked at the service entrance, and emergency wiring stays independent so one fault can't kill both normal and backup power.

In plain terms, the question is: "A sign shall be placed at the service entrance equipment, indicating type and ___ of each on-site emergency power source." Break it into pieces — what equipment, what location or measurement, and what the NEC must say about it — then find the choice that satisfies every piece.

identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.reference_text:
700.7(A) Emergency Sources
A sign shall be placed at the service-entrance equipment, indicating type and location of each on-site emergency power source.
Exception: A sign shall not be required for individual unit equipment as specified in 700.12(H).
records.tip_short: Emergency source signage at the service tells responders the type and location of each on-site source. Correct: D — location. 700.7(A) requires a sign indicating the type and location of each on-site emergency source. Not A: Voltage is not required on the 700.7(A) sign; it requires type and location. Not B: Kilowatt rating is not required on the 700.7(A) sign. Not C: Hours of fuel is not required on the 700.7(A) sign.

Kilowatt rating is not required on the 700.7(A) sign.

records.prompt: Separately installed pressure connectors shall be used with conductors at the ampacities not exceeding the ampacity at the listed and ___ temperature rating of the connector.
records.gist: Terminations are rated for a temperature that limits conductor selection. The question asks which word describes that published rating.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: ampacity, conductors. Start with 110.14(C)(2), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Every splice and terminal must stay tight for decades: torque screws to spec (a loose aluminum terminal starts fires), use pressure connectors only within their listed ampacity, and house all splices in boxes with insulation as good as the wire itself. One iron rule: a ground fault must never be able to start a motor or sneak around a stop button — so switching always goes in the ungrounded leg.

This asks how many amps the conductor may safely carry under the stated conditions. Apply temperature and adjustment factors first, then read the resulting ampacity.

records.reference_text:
110.14(C)(2) Separate Connector Provisions
Separately installed pressure connectors shall be used with conductors at the ampacities not exceeding the ampacity at the listed and identified temperature rating of the connector.
Informational Note: Equipment markings or listing information may additionally restrict the sizing and temperature ratings of connected conductors.
records.tip_short: Separate pressure connectors limit ampacity to their listed and identified temperature rating. Correct: C — identified. 110.14(C)(2) limits ampacity to the listed and identified temperature rating of the connector. Not A: Marked is not the Code wording; 110.14(C)(2) says listed and identified. Not B: Tested is not the Code wording; 110.14(C)(2) says listed and identified. Not D: Certified is not the Code wording; 110.14(C)(2) says listed and identified.

Tested is not the Code wording; 110.14(C)(2) says listed and identified.

records.prompt: The ___ number of branch circuits shall be determined from the total calculated load and the size or rating of the circuits used.
records.gist: The dwelling's required branch-circuit count is the total computed load divided by the circuit rating. The question asks which word fills that blank.

records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: branch circuit, load calculation. Start with 210.11(A), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Load calculations never just add everything up, because a home never runs all loads at once. Start with 3 VA per square foot of living space (outside dimensions, minus open porches and unfinished spaces), add 1,500 VA for each small-appliance and laundry circuit, then shrink the subtotal with the demand factor (first 3,000 VA at full value, 3,001 to 120,000 VA at 35%, the remainder at 25%). Ranges and dryers use their own tables — a range nameplate is only the starting point. Heat and AC: count the larger one, never both.

The minimum number of branch circuits shall be determined from the total calculated load and the size or rating of the circuits used. In all installations, the number of circuits shall be sufficient to supply the load served. In no case shall the load on any circuit exceed the maximum specified by 220.11.

records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Boxes are sized by volume, not vibes: every wire, clamp, and device yoke eats cubic inches, so a crowded box is a Code violation and a fire risk. Device boxes need minimum depth (a flush device needs room behind it), and unused breaker or knockout openings must be closed with listed fillers so fingers and sparks can't get in. Switchboards and panelboards add their own rules: conductors belong only in the section they terminate in, and rear-access gear must say so on the front.

In plain terms, the question is: "A ___ is a portion of a sign that may provide protection from the weather but is not an electrical enclosure." Article 100 Definitions — Sign Body
Sign Body. A portion of a sign that may provide protection from the weather but is not an electrical enclosure. (600) (CMP—18)

Article 100 defines Sign Body as a portion that may protect from weather but is not an electrical enclosure. Not A: Section Sign means a sign built in sections, not the weather-protecting portion. Not C: Sign Gutter is not an Article 100 defined term. Not D: A sign enclosure is electrical, while the definition says it is not an electrical enclosure.

records.prompt: Where a panelboard is supplied through a transformer, the overcurrent protection required by 408.36 shall be located on the ___ side of the transformer.
records.gist: A transformer changes the voltage level, and overcurrent protection is required on a specific side. The question asks which side.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: overcurrent protection, transformer. Start with 408.36(B), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Overcurrent protection works in layers. The branch breaker or fuse handles violent short circuits and ground faults and must carry the motor's starting surge without tripping. Delicate internals — luminaire ballasts, appliance circuits, control wiring — get smaller supplementary protectors, but those never replace branch-circuit protection. Where staying online matters, selective coordination stages the devices so only the faulted circuit goes dark.

This asks you to match this motor or transformer setup to its rule. Subject: transformer. Identify whether the question is about protection size, conductor size, disconnect location, or marking.

LOOKUP FOCUS
overcurrent protection, transformer
records.reference_text:
408.36(B) Supplied Through a Transformer
Where a panelboard is supplied through a transformer, the overcurrent protection required by 408.36 shall be located on the secondary side of the transformer.
Exception: A panelboard supplied by the secondary side of a transformer shall be considered as protected by the overcurrent protection provided on the primary side of the transformer where that protection is in accordance with 240.21(C)(1).
records.tip_short: A panelboard fed through a transformer gets its overcurrent protection on the secondary side, per 408.36(B). Correct: C — secondary. 408.36(B) requires the panelboard overcurrent protection on the secondary side of the transformer. Not A: Supply side is the primary side, but 408.36(B) requires protection on the secondary side. Not B: Primary protection alone is permitted only under the 240.21(C)(1) exception, not as the rule. Not D: High leg is a delta phase conductor, not a transformer side.
choice_notes: Supply side is the primary side, but 408.36(B) requires protection on the secondary side.
Primary protection alone is permitted only under the 240.21(C)(1) exception, not as the rule.
408.36(B) requires the panelboard overcurrent protection on the secondary side of the transformer.
High leg is a delta phase conductor, not a transformer side.

records.prompt: Open equipment doors must not impede access to or from working space required in 110.26. If the door(s) reduce(s) the access to less than ___ inches wide and 6 1/2 feet high, access is considered impeded.
records.gist: Open equipment doors must not block egress; the passage width has a minimum. The question asks how many inches wide.
keywords: identify the equipment, location, and requirement
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: identify the equipment, location, and requirement. Start with 110.26, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Working space is the empty bubble an electrician stands in while servicing live gear — nobody may store boxes or park equipment in it. The NEC measures it three ways: depth in front (3+ ft depending on voltage and what faces the gear — concrete or brick walls facing you mean deeper space), 30 in. minimum width (or the equipment's width), and 6-1/2 ft of headroom. Big gear needs doors that swing 90° and a way out that open doors can't block. Above panels, the space up to the ceiling belongs to electrics only — no pipes or ducts.

This is a minimum-limit question. Numbers in the question: 2 feet. The correct choice is the minimum value the NEC allows — eliminate any choice on the wrong side of that limit.

LOOKUP FOCUS

records.reference_text:
110.26 Spaces About Electrical Equipment
Working space, and access to and egress from working space, shall be provided and maintained about all electrical equipment to permit ready and safe operation and maintenance of such equipment. Open equipment doors shall not impede access to and egress from the working space. Access or egress is impeded if one or more simultaneously opened equipment doors restrict working space access to be less than 610 mm (24 in.) wide and 2.0 m (6 1/2 ft) high.
(A) Working Space
Working space for equipment operating at 1000 volts, nominal, or less to ground and likely to require examination, adjustment, servicing, or maintenance while energized shall comply with the dimensions of 110.26(A)(1), (A)(2), (A)(3), and (A)(4) or as required or permitted elsewhere in this Code.
records.tip_short: Open equipment doors can't squeeze the working-space access below 24 inches wide by 6 1/2 feet high. Correct: B — 24. 110.26 says access is impeded if doors restrict it to less than 610 mm (24 inches) wide. Not A: 18 inches is too narrow; 110.26 uses 610 mm (24 inches). Not C: 30 inches is the working space width, not the door access limit. Not D: 36 inches is a working space depth value, not the door access limit.
choice_notes: 18 inches is too narrow; 110.26 uses 610 mm (24 inches).
110.26 says access is impeded if doors restrict it to less than 610 mm (24 inches) wide.

36 inches is a working space depth value, not the door access limit.

records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: cable. Start with 400.36, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Flexible cords are temporary wiring, not a substitute for fixed circuits — they must stay continuous (no splices except repairing hard-service cord), stay short, and match the job's toughness: junior hard-service (SJ) for light duty, hard-service (S, ST) for tools and appliances, extra-hard (SO) for construction sites. The letters are a code: O = oil-resistant, T = thermoplastic, W = weather/wet-location plus sunlight-resistant. A cord in a wet place outdoors needs that W — which is why STOOW is the answer there.

WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Branch circuits are rated by their breaker: the standard sizes are 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, and 50 amps. A multiwire (shared-neutral) circuit must open all its ungrounded legs together so no leg can stay live alone. In plain terms, the question is: "Where a building or structure has any combination of feeders, branch circuits, or services passing through it or supplying it, a permanent…" Subject: feeder. records.prompt: In a concealed knob-and-tube wiring system, a minimum clearance of ___ must be maintained between conductors.
records.gist: Concealed knob-and-tube conductors run open on insulators inside walls and ceilings, so air space keeps them apart. The question asks the minimum spacing between the conductors.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: conductors. Start with 394.19(A), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Decode the letters first: EMT = Electrical Metallic Tubing (thin-wall, hand-bendable). RMC = Rigid Metal Conduit (thick threaded steel). IMC = Intermediate (in between). FMC = Flexible Metal Conduit (bendable whip). ENT = Electrical Nonmetallic Tubing (blue smurf tube). LFMC = Liquidtight Flexible Metal (sealed whip). RNC = Rigid Nonmetallic Conduit (PVC). Rules answer three things: clearance from wood framing (1-1/4 in. or a nail plate), burial depth, and strapping (within a foot of every box, then every few feet by type).

This is a minimum-limit question. The correct choice is the minimum value the NEC allows — eliminate any choice on the wrong side of that limit.

conductors

394.19(A) General
A clearance of not less than 75 mm (3 in.) shall be maintained between conductors and a clearance of not less than 25 mm (1 in.) between the conductor and the surface over which it passes.

Correct: B — 3". 394.19(A) requires a clearance of not less than 75 mm (3 inches) between conductors. Not A: 2 inches is too little; 394.19(A) requires at least 3 inches between conductors. Not C: 4 inches is more than the minimum; 394.19(A) requires only 3 inches between conductors. Not D: 6 inches is double the 3-inch minimum that 394.19(A) sets between conductors.

records.prompt: Table ___ lists the minimum size equipment grounding conductors.
records.gist: Article 250 has several sizing tables, each for a different kind of grounding or bonding conductor. The question asks which table sizes the equipment grounding conductor run with a circuit.
records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: equipment grounding conductor, conductors. Start with Table 250.122, then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three jobs, three parts. Grounding connects the system to the earth (rods, plates, concrete-encased electrodes) to drain lightning and surges. Bonding joins all the metal parts together so fault current has a fast low-resistance road back to the source that trips the breaker. The grounded conductor (neutral, white) carries normal current; the grounding conductor (green/bare) carries only fault current. The main bonding jumper is where neutral and ground meet — at the service, and only there.

This is a minimum-limit question. The correct choice is the minimum value the NEC allows — eliminate any choice on the wrong side of that limit.

LOOKUP FOCUS
equipment grounding conductor, conductors

Table 250.122 Minimum Size Equipment Grounding Conductors for Grounding Raceway and Equipment
Copper, aluminum, or copper-clad aluminum equipment grounding conductors of the wire type shall not be smaller than shown in Table 250.122.
records.tip_short: Equipment grounding conductors are sized from Table 250.122 by the rating of the overcurrent device ahead of the circuit. Correct: D — 250.122.
choice_notes: Table 250.66 sizes the grounding electrode conductor from the service conductor size, not the equipment grounding conductor.
Table 250.94 covers the intersystem bonding and the bonding conductor for communication systems, not equipment grounding conductors.
Table 250.102(C)(1) sizes the grounded conductor, main bonding jumper, system bonding jumper, and supply-side bonding jumper.

records.prompt: Informational Note: ANSI ___-2017, Product Safety Signs and Labels, provides guidelines for suitable font sizes, words, colors, symbols, and location requirements for labels.
records.gist: Field-applied warning labels must use effective words, colors, and symbols, and an informational note points to an ANSI standard for the details. The question asks the number of that product safety sign and label standard.

records.lookup_summary: Lookup clues: identify the equipment, location, and requirement. Start with 110.21(B), then read the matching subsection and exceptions.
records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three formulas run the math questions. Ohm's law: volts = amps × ohms. Power: watts = volts × amps (so amps = watts ÷ volts). Resistors in parallel combine as the product over the sum. Voltage drop percent is volts lost ÷ source volts. And AC frequency: 60 cycles per second means one full 360° wave takes 1/60 s. To turn a percent into a fraction, write it over 100 and reduce.

This asks which conductor color the NEC allows here. Recall which colors are reserved (grounded, grounding) and which remain for ungrounded conductors.

records.reference_text:
110.21(B) Field-Applied Hazard Markings
Where caution, warning, or danger hazard markings such as labels or signs are required by this Code, the markings shall meet the following requirements:
The marking shall be of sufficient durability to withstand the environment involved and warn of the hazards using effective words, colors, symbols, or any combination thereof.
Informational Note No. 2: See ANSI Z535.4-2011 (R2017), Product Safety Signs and Labels, which details the design, application, use, and placement of safety signs and labels on a wide variety of products.

Z541.B is not the standard cited in 110.21(B); product safety labels are in the ANSI Z535 family.

WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS

records.prompt: For motors marked with design letters B, C, or D, conductors having a higher insulation rating shall be permitted to be used, provided the ampacity of such conductors does not exceed the ___ ampacity.

records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
A motor circuit has two separate protections doing two jobs. The overload device (heaters, overload relay) guards against a motor slowly cooking from too much load — sized from the motor's own nameplate amps (125% for sturdy motors, 115% for the rest), with one overload unit per phase (three units on a three-phase motor). The breaker or fuses handle violent short circuits and ground faults. The controller starts and stops the motor; the disconnect within sight of the motor lets a worker be sure it cannot restart while hands are on it.

Three formulas run the math questions. Ohm's law: volts = amps × ohms. Power: watts = volts × amps (so amps = watts ÷ volts). Resistors in parallel combine as the product over the sum. records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS

Three jobs, three parts. Grounding connects the system to the earth (rods, plates, concrete-encased electrodes) to drain lightning and surges. Three formulas run the math questions. Ohm's law: volts = amps × ohms. Power: watts = volts × amps (so amps = watts ÷ volts). Resistors in parallel combine as the product over the sum. records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Three jobs, three parts. Grounding connects the system to the earth (rods, plates, concrete-encased electrodes) to drain lightning and surges. Bonding joins all the metal parts together so fault current has a fast low-resistance road back to the source that trips the breaker. The grounded conductor (neutral, white) carries normal current; the grounding conductor (green/bare) carries only fault current. The main bonding jumper is where neutral and ground meet — at the service, and only there.

records.prompt: According to the State Electrical Act and Board rules, it is the electrical contractor's responsibility to call the inspector to schedule which of the following types of inspections during the project?
records.gist: State inspectors come out at several stages of a project, but only when someone tells them the work is ready. The question asks which inspection requests are the electrical contractor's job.

records.info_tip:
WHAT THIS QUESTION MEANS
PLAIN-LANGUAGE BACKGROUND
Work under state inspection starts with a request for inspection filed with the State Electrical Board. The State Electrical Board Rules (Title 100 of the Nebraska Administrative Code) then say who must call the inspector as the job moves along.

records.reference_text:
Title 100 NAC Rule 13 Requests for Inspection
It is the responsibility of the installer or electrical contractor to notify the inspector at such times as the project is ready for inspection. ... (1) rough-in inspections necessary prior to the concealment of wiring, and (2) final inspections, and (3) re-inspection required by the issuance of a "correction order". The requirement of timely notification is an ongoing responsibility of the installer or electrical contractor during the entire life of the project. Notification must be made by telephone request, email request, on-line request, or text message to the area State Electrical Inspector.
Neb. Rev. Stat. 81-2134(2) Where wiring is to be concealed, the inspector must be notified within reasonable time to complete a rough-in inspection prior to concealment, exclusive of Saturdays, Sundays, and holidays.
records.tip_short: Calling the inspector is the contractor's job at every stage: before cover, at the end, and after a correction order. Correct: D — all of these. Rule 13 makes the installer or electrical contractor notify the inspector for rough-in inspections before wiring is concealed, final inspections, and re-inspections required by a correction order. Not A: Rough-in is only one of the three inspections Rule 13 makes the contractor call for. Not B: Finals are only one of the three inspections Rule 13 makes the contractor call for. Not C: Correction-order re-inspections are only one of the three inspections Rule 13 makes the contractor call for.
